#5473. Google told schools to accept AI or lose Search. Now 3 of America’s 4 largest districts are pushing back

Google has handed school districts what many have called an ultimatum: Allow students to see AI summaries in their Google searches, or give up Google Search on school accounts altogether.

In August, Google switched on a Gemini tab in Google Classroom by default for K-12 students whose schools had already allowed its AI chatbot, Gemini. On Nov. 3, it reversed course, announcing that its AI tools will be off for K-12 student accounts unless school administrators turn them on, starting early next year. But Google also made clear that schools that want students to have Google Search will have to accept AI Overviews, the AI-generated summaries that have become a familiar sight at the top of search results.

“Search and AI are deeply integrated,” Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told The New York Times, adding that students at schools that don’t allow AI “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”

Google’s decision comes as tech companies face mounting legal pressure over harm to children. In March, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and Google’s YouTube negligent and determined they failed to warn users about the dangers of their platforms. In January, Google and Character.AI, a chatbot company with ties to Google, agreed to settle lawsuits from families who said their children were harmed by its chatbots.

And earlier this month, a family sued Google, alleging their 13-year-old daughter used Gemini on her school-issued Chromebook to plan her suicide and that Google pushed its AI products on students without warning parents or schools.

“We hear parents and teachers’ concerns about students using AI to shortcut learning, and we share the same goal: help students learn,” a Google spokesperson said, adding that the company is piloting new Gemini features to support “productive struggle” by helping students “work through problems without skipping straight to answers.”

Whether that’s enough to win over districts that have restricted AI is another question. The country’s four largest school districts have landed in different places, both on AI and on Google’s decision to tie it to Search.

Alphabet, Google’s parent company, did not respond to Fortune‘s request for comment.

On Nov. 11, about 30 protesters gathered outside Google’s West Loop office, chanting, “Hey Google, nice try. We don’t want your Gemini.”

In a statement to the Chicago Sun-Times, a CPS spokesperson said the district is “actively exploring all options to independently suppress” the AI Overviews in Google searches.

“The District would like to continue to provide students with access to the Google search engine without the AI component. If such an arrangement can’t be reached, the District will look to other search solutions,” the spokesperson said.

New York City Public Schools, the nation’s largest district, appears headed in a similar direction, though it has yet to decide. On Sept. 2, Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels announced a one-year moratorium on student-facing AI for 2-K through eighth grade. They also banned companion chatbots in all grades.

After Google’s announcement, Mamdani posted on X that “Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools. No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children.”

City Council Speaker Julie Menin and Council Member Shekar Krishnan sent a letter to Google CEO Sundar Pichai asking whether Google would let students keep using Google Search without AI Overviews and, if not, why not, given Google’s record of restricting product features for young users, as it does with YouTube Kids. The stakes are large: The district has about 1.3 million Chromebooks, including 500,000 assigned to students, according to the letter.

District spokesperson Nicole Brownstein told Gothamist that officials are “reaching out to Google to discuss this update further,” and that the district had already disabled the Gemini chatbot and AI Mode on student Chromebooks. If Google doesn’t budge, the nation’s largest school district will have to choose between softening its stance and finding another search engine.

Los Angeles Unified, the nation’s second-largest district, announced on Sept. 2 that it would block generative AI for students in all grades on district-issued devices for the 2026-27 school year, a move affecting an estimated 378,000 students.

During public comment at a district Generative AI Ad Hoc Committee meeting after Google’s announcement, Hillary Power, a parent and member of Schools Beyond Screens, called for Los Angeles Unified to continue “formalizing, extending and expanding the current T-K to 12 moratorium of student use of generative AI.”

“Google has been particularly clear on their priorities when several days ago they issued a monopolistic and, frankly, pathetic ultimatum to schools to use their AI search products or be cut off,” she continued.

The district has asked Google for a way to turn off the AI summaries, according to LAist, and said it is reviewing Google’s announcement and its “potential implications for schools, educators and students.”

Miami-Dade County Public Schools, the nation’s third-largest district, may be headed in a different direction.

In 2023, the district blocked AI chatbots such as ChatGPT over concerns about cheating and misinformation, according to The New York Times. Two years later, it reversed course, offering Gemini for Education to about 100,000 high school students, the largest AI deployment in a U.S. school district at the time. In February, the district announced a continued collaboration with Google to give all its high school students free access to full-length SAT practice exams through Gemini.

But on Sept. 16, the Florida Board of Education voted to require public school districts and charter schools to set rules for AI use. Schools will also have to tell parents and guardians which AI tools students will interact with, so families can opt their child into a tool or request a non-AI alternative. Districts have until July 1, 2027, to comply.

Miami-Dade County Public Schools did not respond to questions about how it will adapt to Google’s policy and the new Florida rules.

Former Federal Trade Commission chair Lina Khan criticized Google’s decision to tie Search to its AI summaries. In a Nov. 3 post on X, she said the company is using its search monopoly to “coerce schools into adopting AI.”

“Multiple courts have found Google liable for violating antitrust laws, and this latest move shows it remains unchastened,” she said. “As the public increasingly pushes back against the use of AI in schools, Google is making it clear it will punish those who don’t fall in line.”

Khan isn’t the only one questioning whether the move is legal. Zephyr Teachout, a professor at Fordham Law School, said she does not find Google’s claim that it cannot unlink AI Overviews from Search “credible,” and that the company could be found to violate antitrust laws governing how companies tie the sale of two products.

In antitrust law, “tying” is when a company with significant market power requires customers who want one of its products to take another as well. Google’s parent, Alphabet, is No. 5 on the 2026 Fortune 500. According to the FTC, tying raises antitrust questions when it “restricts competition without providing benefits to consumers.”

“Google ran search for decades without AI, has filters that allow people to see results without AI summaries, and has been inconsistent in how it has responded to the tying claim — merely asserting they are ‘deeply integrated’ is not a legal argument,” Teachout said. “The company has on/off controls for K-12 administrators and could have an on/off control for search and AI.”

Google has lost a tying case before. In April 2025, U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema found that Google had been “willfully acquiring and maintaining monopoly power” in two parts of the online advertising market and that it had illegally tied them together by pushing websites that wanted full access to its ad exchange to also use its ad server.

But the company has also won a case involving AI Overviews. In September, U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta dismissed a lawsuit by Penske Media over Google’s use of its content for AI Overviews, finding that Penske had not plausibly shown that Search and AI Overviews were separate products.

Teachout said schools are different, pointing to the “clear evidence of a separate market demand in schools for search as distinct from AI.”

Whether a court ever takes up such a case, or agrees with Teachout, is an open question. Google’s changes take effect early next year, and until then, districts have to decide whether keeping Google Search is worth accepting the AI that comes with it.

#5472. Microsoft jabs at OpenAI and Anthropic, touting cheaper, customizable AI models of its own

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:57 amNovember 17, 2026 at 12:33 pm

Microsoft is a partner and investor in both OpenAI and Anthropic, and it sells their AI models to its own customers. But another role was on full display during the company’s Ignite keynote Tuesday: competitor.

“Simply stated, anything you can do in Claude or ChatGPT, you can do better with Copilot and for less,” said Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft’s commercial business, during the opening keynote at the company’s annual conference for IT professionals and business customers in San Francisco.

Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, went further. “We’ve all seen Anthropic and OpenAI embrace documents, slides, and spreadsheets, but their simplified viewers and editors force compromise on power and collaboration,” he said.

The full versions of Word, Excel and PowerPoint inside Copilot are included in the subscription. “That means that Copilot is the only way to draft a PowerPoint presentation without spinning a meter,” Andreou said.

Microsoft’s cost comparison: Andreou backed up the pitch with a chart of estimated monthly costs per business user, including subscription and usage fees. It put Copilot at $30 for an “everyday” AI user, compared with $81 for ChatGPT and $205 for Claude.

For “advanced” users of each company’s agent tools, it showed $96 for Copilot, $149 for ChatGPT and $299 for Claude. Most of the Claude figure is estimated usage charges on top of Anthropic’s $20 enterprise seat.

The numbers come from research Microsoft commissioned and paid for from GigaOm, based on testing Microsoft ran in October on modeled workloads. They reflect enterprise pricing, which adds usage charges to a per-seat fee, not the flat monthly subscriptions that individuals pay for ChatGPT and Claude.

Partners and rivals: The pitch comes as Anthropic expands into Microsoft’s core business. Last week it introduced new Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards that compete more directly with Office. The company is expected to make its IPO this week, putting new scrutiny on its financials and long-term growth prospects.

The companies’ products are also intertwined. Anthropic’s Claude for Microsoft 365, for example, lets people use Claude inside Office apps for tasks such as sorting email and creating slide decks.

The product has less than a tenth as many weekly users as the paid version of Copilot in Office, The Information reported Monday, citing internal Microsoft data. Andreou is one of the executives who see that as a sign Microsoft can keep customers from switching, the report said.

New MAI models: Microsoft AI also released a new batch of its own MAI models, built to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic for a fraction of the price. It’s a notable stance, given that Microsoft still sells their models, too. On the same stage, CEO Satya Nadella announced that OpenAI’s GPT-6.2, released Tuesday morning, is now available in Microsoft Foundry.

The lineup includes MAI Code 2, available in GitHub Copilot starting Tuesday. Microsoft says it delivers 96% of the coding performance of Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the price, on benchmarks Microsoft chose.

Microsoft also introduced MAI Cyber 2 Flash, a security model it says matches OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra on one benchmark at less than 2% of the cost per task. Other new models cover image editing, live speech and transcription.

The other new business: MAI Licensed Weights. Companies can take a Microsoft AI model, customize it with their own data and run it in their own Azure environment, with help from Microsoft’s Frontier Company consulting arm. AT&T used an earlier version of the program, Custom Models, to build a MAI model for 5G network analytics.

It’s the latest step in Microsoft’s push for what Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman has called “long term self-sufficiency,” which started with seven homegrown models at Build in June.

Keeping costs in check: The cost theme ran through the keynote. In a demo, Althoff showed Copilot building a keynote outline, a slide deck and a customer tracker for a retail conference, plus an agent he named Amelia to keep the work going.

The cost of his two-hour Sunday session: about 10,000 credits, or roughly $100. Althoff presented that as a bargain compared with the staff time it would have taken: “my team hits the ground running for NRF without me bothering them,” he said.

Microsoft is also selling tools to keep that bill in check. A new Agent 365 Business Analytics feature shows business leaders what’s driving their AI spending and what they’re getting for it, and a companion Cost Management tool lets IT set spending policies and get alerts. Microsoft cited a McKinsey survey in which 93% of respondents reported exceeding their AI budgets.

In another notable announcement, Microsoft and Salesforce unveiled “Copilotforce,” bringing Salesforce customer data and actions into Copilot, Teams and Fabric. The Copilot plugin is available in preview.

Earlier, Nadella opened the keynote by addressing last week’s global Outlook outage.

#5471. Private equity–backed companies face a $300 billion debt wall. They’re looking at your retirement account for an exit

The private credit and private equity industries currently face two huge problems. First, the private equity industry sits on a nine-year backlog of holdings that it wishes it could IPO or sell to other companies, but because of recent poor performance it cannot seem to offload these positions. PitchBook has reported that while private equity funds look to exit positions in three to five years, 30% of all holdings out there have been sitting on private equity balance sheets for six or more years (a record high).

Second, private equity–backed companies face a $300 billion wall of debt coming due in 2028 and 2029. Normally, this would not be an issue, but almost all of this debt was refinanced in 2020 and 2021, when interest rates were near zero, and now will need to be refinanced at far higher rates, with no clear buyers in sight.

Both of these problems together signal desperate times for the private credit and private equity industries. If traditional channels of financing are not going to work, then they must find another source of non-traditional financing to offload these positions to.

And, the private asset industry may have found just the unsuspecting party – retail investors. Given the recent changes in the definition of “sophisticated investors” who were the standard investors that were allowed to invest in private equity/credit and rollbacks in enforcement of vehicles that could hold such products, retail investors are now at the front lines to be force-fed these products through clever marketing.

Not only are private credit and private equity holdings showing up in ETFs and mutual funds, they are showing up in new products like perpetuals that are highly en vogue among retail investors. Even more nefarious, private credit is slowly making its way into 401(k) plans at the behest of the White House, which has pitched it to investors as an effort to “Democratize access to private assets.”

Now, why is this all so bad? If markets are efficient, then retail investors will just be paying a fair price for such assets, correct? Well, with private credit and private equity assets, no one knows the fair price because they are unlisted and non-traded. Traditionally, it takes months of due diligence by experts to come to a correct price for each individual asset when it is sold in an IPO or to another firm. Now, we are to assume retail investors can do this analysis on illiquid assets in hours or minutes to determine if it is right for them to hold – not likely.

Aside from the hard-to-value issue, private assets also come with higher fees. The traditional 2 and 20 fee structure (2% of AUM and 20% of profits) will surely be passed on to retail investors in whatever form the private asset takes in their portfolio. These costs far surpass the average ETF expense ratio of 0.2% in the large-cap equity space. To see how expensive it can get, WisdomTree offers a private credit ETF (ticker HYIN) with an annual expense ratio of 4.34%. That means the fund itself needs to return more than 4.34% a year just for an investor to break even. Next, aside from fees, these private assets understate their inherent risk through a process Cliff Asness has dubbed “volatility laundering.” So if they claim the risk of the product is equivalent to a low-risk bond, it may exhibit the risk of a small-cap equity.

Finally, some high-end investors have already begun to see how these investments can turn sour. Over the summer, many high-net-worth investors asked to redeem their money from several BDCs and other private credit funds. These withdrawal requests were denied (above the contractual level permitted) – what investors thought was a safe place to store money in a deposit-like instrument turned out to be far riskier than they thought.

In all, opacity, high cost, terms to redemption and volatility laundering all spell potential doom for retail investors if they buy into these private asset products, and they need to be on high alert when such products are offered to them as long-term, safe investments for their retirement funds.

The opinions expressed in Fortune.com commentary pieces are solely the views of their authors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions and beliefs of Fortune.

Derek Horstmeyer is a professor of finance at George Mason University’s Costello College of Business, specializing in corporate finance. His research focuses on boards, ETF and mutual fund performance, and hedge fund activism. He helped create and lead the first student-managed investment fund at GMU, founded and serves as director of the Future of Finance Lab, and serves on the board of the Washington Association of Money Managers.

#5470. Seattle startup Aarden raises $8M to help landowners navigate the AI and energy building boom

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 1:36 pmNovember 20, 2026 at 5:15 pm

Seattle startup Aarden AI on Tuesday announced $8 million in new funding to grow its team and accelerate its work helping landowners evaluate potential uses for their properties and navigate deals with developers building data centers, clean energy projects, housing and other projects.

Founded last year, the company says its clients collectively own or manage approximately 14 million acres worldwide — nearly the land area of West Virginia. Aarden’s team said it has evaluated more than $500 million worth of land deals.

“But land markets remain opaque and manual with far too much friction. Finding the right site, and building trust with the right partners quickly, is more important than ever for our economy and our environment,” founder and CEO Danan Margason said in a statement.

The company combines data on hundreds of land attributes with historical market data and proprietary models to assess development suitability, valuation trends, ownership and community sentiment. Its tools and services also help developers identify sites and connect with landowners.

Aarden generates revenue through subscriptions to its technology, which includes AI-native data, models and investment tools, and through fees for services tied to specific deals or analyses.

The new funding brings Aarden’s total investments to $12 million. Overture Ventures led the round, with participation from Madrona and Propeller Ventures. The startup previously raised $4 million in a round led by Planeteer in June 2025. The company has 13 employees and plans to nearly double in size over the next 12 months.

Margason said he launched the business on the premise that while there have long been tools to support developers, landowners have been largely on their own to evaluate and optimize deals so they’re not taken advantage of or end up partnering with untrustworthy organizations.

One customer, timberland investment manager Resource Management Service, uses Aarden to evaluate whether tracts are best suited for continued timber production, conservation, solar development or other uses.

“Diligence that used to take months now produces investment-grade answers we can act on, and that is shaping how we manage value across our portfolio,” said Alex Hinson, president and CEO of Resource Management Service.

Other companies offering property research and analysis tools include Acres, which provides land data, valuations and due diligence tools, and Land id, which offers property insights and mapping tools.

Ben Eidelson, a partner at Stepchange Ventures, which participated in the startup’s first funding round, said the company is already having an impact.

“We now have the capability to make smarter decisions about land, optimizing for the outcomes that matter from conservation to the local economy,” Eidelson said on LinkedIn.

#5469. ‘Do not search Amazon’: Meta’s Muse now shops elsewhere by default

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 2:36 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 9:45 am

Two months after Amazon slammed the door on Muse, the AI agent has stopped knocking.

The shopping skill that guides Muse, Meta’s personal AI agent, now tells it to “leave out Amazon unless the user asks for it,” according to the instructions Muse provides when asked. The instructions include a template brief for Muse’s browser that says, “Do not search Amazon.”

The change was spotted last week by Juozas Kaziukenas, founder of the e-commerce research firm Marketplace Pulse, who asked Muse for the text of its shopping skill and compared it with the version from the day before. He posted the before-and-after on Friday. GeekWire asked Muse for its shopping skill and got the same language.

“Amazon blocked Muse, so now Muse blocked Amazon,” Kaziukenas wrote on X.

Muse is also told not to name Amazon as a site to search in that browser brief, “even as an example,” unless the user asked for Amazon. The skill steers the agent to Walmart and Target for general goods, Best Buy for electronics, and Home Depot or Lowe’s for home improvement.

For Muse users, not much changes in practice. Amazon began blocking Muse in September, less than two weeks after Meta launched the agent, showing anyone who tried to shop through it a message saying continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon’s Conditions of Use. Kaziukenas said any Amazon search would fail anyway because of the block.

What’s new is that Meta appears to be going along with what Amazon asked for. When it began blocking Muse, Amazon said it had asked Meta to “remove Amazon from the experience.” Meta hadn’t said publicly how it would respond.

Meta didn’t respond to an inquiry about the change. An Amazon spokesperson said the company had nothing to share.

Amazon objected that Muse didn’t identify itself when it browsed the site and appeared to capture and store customer credentials. Meta has said Muse has no visibility into people’s passwords or payment methods. The standoff set off a broader debate over who owns the customer relationship when an AI agent does the buying.

Since then, both sides have kept moving. More than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada signed up for Muse in its first six weeks, Forbes reported, and Walmart, Best Buy, Sephora and Wayfair are among the retailers working with Meta on it.

The business stakes are high for Amazon. It generated more than $68 billion in advertising revenue last year, including sponsored products that appear as people browse its pages — ads a shopper might never see if an outside agent does the searching. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said Muse will take a small cut of the transactions it handles.

Amazon has fought this battle before, suing Perplexity last November over the shopping agent in its Comet browser. It’s now pressing that case in part on the same Conditions of Use it cited in blocking Muse.

On Amazon’s earnings call last month, CEO Andy Jassy said outside shopping agents aren’t making a meaningful dent in Amazon’s advertising business. “Few customers are doing much shopping this way yet,” he said, adding that the experience still isn’t great or more convenient than going straight to a retailer.

Jassy said Amazon expects to work with “horizontal agents,” general-purpose assistants like Muse, but believes its own Alexa for Shopping will be the main agent people use to shop Amazon. Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping in May, combining its Rufus shopping chatbot with the Alexa+ assistant.

It has since started letting some customers text Alexa to shop, much as people do with Muse.

#5468. Institutional trading on Kalshi jumped 4,124% in six months. How much of it is hedging is unclear

Institutional trading in prediction-market contracts on Kalshi reached $26.3 billion in October, up from $622.7 million in April, according to figures the company provided to Fortune. That is a 4,124% increase in six months.

The growth is staggering. Less clear is how much of that money hedges economic risk and how much is trading, much of it on sports.

Kalshi counted 822 institutional accounts that had traded, up from 312 in April, with 242 trading more than $1 million a month. The figures exclude Kalshi’s perpetual futures business, market makers, designated liquidity providers, and internal accounts.

Nearly all of the $26.3 billion came from regular order-book trading rather than negotiated block trades, the company told Fortune.

Across the platform, sports dominate. Combo and sports contracts made up about 85% of Kalshi’s volume in the 30 days before Nov. 20, while financial and economics contracts together accounted for less than 1%, according to Ticker Tracker’s Kalshi volume data. Those figures cover all traders, not only institutions, and are based on face value.

Eric Zitzewitz, a Dartmouth College economics professor who studies prediction markets, told Fortune in an email that institutions trading on these platforms fall into three groups. Some make markets and mostly seek to balance their books, while others respond to requests for quotes on parlays and take the other side.

A third group trades single-event markets against small traders’ behavioral biases, such as overpricing longshots. His impression, he said, is that all three are becoming more involved.

Andy Ross, a former Standard Chartered executive who became Kalshi’s head of institutional business in March, pointed to the hedge funds that have joined or are preparing to join the platform. “If you added all of the AUM of those hedge funds together, they would have over a trillion dollars in AUM, which is massive,” he told Fortune.

That is their total assets under management, not the amount invested on Kalshi. Ross named AQR Capital Management as one firm “actively looking at” prediction markets. “We are exploring whether our models are suited to trading prediction markets directly,” AQR said in a written response to Fortune.

The approaches vary. Some funds are testing contracts with small trading teams, Ross said, while others use prediction-market data to build systematic strategies, and some trade event contracts actively.

Franklin Templeton is an example of the data-only approach. The asset manager does not invest directly in prediction markets or take positions on the outcomes of specific events, a company spokesperson told Fortune, but feeds their data into its investment views through a proprietary agentic analyst. “Prediction markets can provide valuable insights into investor sentiment and market expectations,” the spokesperson added.

Ross described election-related block trades, in which a fund could trade a political outcome directly rather than shorting stocks that may move for unrelated reasons. He would not identify the investors. Revealing them, he said, would mean “we wouldn’t have an exchange for very long.”

One of Kalshi’s first customized block trades came in April, when an environmental hedge fund used a contract tied to California’s carbon allowance auction. Bloomberg reported the trade, which Houston-based broker Greenlight Commodities arranged with liquidity from Jump Trading.

John Conlon, a Greenlight director who has spent 30 years in energy, mainly brokering and trading natural gas futures and options, told Fortune that the firm first pitched prediction markets to its longtime power and gas clients. He expected they “would come in and do something simple for the proof of concept,” such as a small trade on weekly natural gas storage data. Nobody did.

Instead, the first trade came from Fathom Energy, a Houston environmental hedge fund run by his friend Francisco Padua, Conlon said.

Greenlight has brokered trades on Kalshi ranging from $25,000 to $7 million, typically $100,000 to $250,000, and had about five active trading parties at the time of the interview.

“Every trade that we have brokered thus far has been a bona fide hedge,” Conlon said. “It won’t be that way forever.” But the brokerage generally does not know its clients’ underlying positions, which makes it impossible to quantify how much the trades saved.

Conlon sees event contracts as a way to hedge risks that traditional derivatives cannot isolate. “If you’re worried about an event or structure, there’s no more simple or true or more surgical hedge than an event contract,” he said.

Corporate hedges are emerging too. In November, Tomorrow Recycling, a Mecha-backed recycler, hedged cardboard prices with Kalshi contracts tied to a U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics index, with Susquehanna Predictions structuring and pricing the trade.

“Hedging prices in our industry has historically been done through privately negotiated arrangements, which were reserved for the bigger players in the industry,” chief financial officer Josh Branham said in written responses to Fortune. The company declined to disclose the size or cost of its position.

“We see this becoming a regular part of how we manage the business,” Branham said. “We’re approaching it thoughtfully because it’s still a relatively new market, and we want to understand how the contracts perform against our actual exposure before committing to anything on a larger scale.”

The examples build on hedges Fortune has covered. In October, a Los Angeles restaurant group operating 25 bars placed a $60,000 hedge on the Dodgers’ postseason, and in August, Kalshi partnered with Blanket, a tool that helps smaller companies find contracts to offset business risks.

Also in October, Susquehanna Predictions priced a Kalshi tungsten hedge for an Ohio metals distributor. Ross distinguished such specialized hedges from the strategies of the largest asset managers, saying cardboard and tungsten contracts could serve midsize companies without necessarily drawing the biggest hedge funds.

Customized block trades like Greenlight’s are a sliver of the $26.3 billion. Nearly all of it trades on Kalshi’s regular order book, where public data does not show which trades come from institutions or what they are betting on.

Karl Whelan, a University College Dublin economics professor who researches prediction markets, said Kalshi’s trade data does not identify counterparties or classify them as institutions, individuals, or market makers, so you have to “take them at their word.”

“The growth in institutional involvement appears to mainly be funds (and sportsbooks) offering parlay bets to retail takers,” he said. Parlays have historically been highly profitable for sportsbooks, he explained, which leaves room for big profits while still undercutting the sportsbooks somewhat, particularly with customers in California, Texas, and other states without legal sportsbooks.

That market is large. Prediction markets handled about 27% of U.S. legal sports-betting volume in the first month of this summer’s World Cup, according to H2 Gambling Capital estimates.

“I don’t think there is substantial economic hedging activity taking place on Kalshi,” Whelan said. “Despite occasional claims to the contrary, very little economic activity hinges on events like whether the Bills beat the Giants or whether Josh Allen scores two touchdowns.”

Kalshi’s fully collateralized structure requires participants to commit funds against potential losses, unlike the margin used in many conventional derivatives markets. That can discourage liquidity providers and widen spreads.

“The only thing we’re missing is margin,” Conlon said. Some prospective corporate clients, including energy companies, also cannot trade yet because event contracts have not cleared their internal risk and compliance reviews, he added.

For now, Kalshi is waiving fees to draw participants. Block trades generate no exchange fee revenue under an incentive program, Ross said, while brokers such as Greenlight collect commissions. The exchange expects to introduce a longer-term pricing structure.

Much of Kalshi’s trading also sits in contracts whose legal status is unsettled. States argue that sports event contracts are illegal gambling, and New Jersey has asked the Supreme Court to take up the question, with the NFL urging the justices to back state gambling rules. In October, the CFTC proposed explicitly defining such contracts as swaps under its jurisdiction.

The 4,124% jump measures how much institutions trade on Kalshi. It does not capture firms like Franklin Templeton that only use its prices, and it does not show how much of the trading is hedging.

The hedges that Kalshi and its brokers point to are real. For now, they are a small part of what institutions trade there.

#5466. Jeff Bezos has some advice for Nvidia’s board on its CEO search

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 5:05 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 9:50 am

Jeff Bezos says Nvidia should look inside the company for its next CEO, and he doesn’t give an outsider much chance of success. The Amazon founder, now co-CEO of AI engineering startup Prometheus, made the comments Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event.

“If you don’t bring Jensen back, I would not hire an outsider. Nvidia is too complicated,” Bezos said. Outside CEOs at complex companies, he added, “have a vanishingly small chance of succeeding,” and he would consider hiring one “a last resort.”

Nvidia’s board says it has no plans to bring Huang back. Harvey Jones, the longtime director named the company’s first board chair last week, opened Nvidia’s earnings call Tuesday afternoon by saying the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”

Jones said the search will include internal and external candidates, and that the board wants a permanent CEO in place quickly but won’t rush the pick.

Huang, the Nvidia co-founder and CEO for 33 years, had posted a statement on X that morning offering to return. He said he had “made serious mistakes” in his personal life and would cooperate with the board’s independent investigation.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote.

Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation last Thursday, a day after the New York Times reported that he’d had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Days earlier, he admitted to an affair with a woman who U.S. officials believe was recruited by Chinese intelligence, according to the Wall Street Journal.

CFO Colette Kress, who spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career, is interim CEO.

Two major Nvidia investors, Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker, asked the board to leave open “the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives wrote in a note Sunday that talk of a Huang comeback is “ridiculous.”

The Amazon precedent (not really): Bezos has been through a founder handoff of his own. He turned over the Amazon CEO job in 2021 to Andy Jassy, a longtime insider who built AWS. When Semafor raised the comparison, Bezos called it a poor one, saying there has never been a more carefully planned transition.

He said he didn’t know enough about what happened in Nvidia’s board meetings to say whether Huang should return. But he called Huang a remarkable founder who deserves “admiration and respect no matter what.”

Huang himself said in a Bloomberg interview recorded Oct. 14 that he hoped his successor was already inside the company.

The Nvidia comments came in a wide-ranging interview. Bezos also said Blue Origin is using Prometheus tools on two projects, called President Trump by far the most communicative of the presidents he has worked with, and said Robert Pattinson was the clear choice to play the next James Bond after screen tests of five finalists.

Business as usual, officially: Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier, including $107.6 billion from its data center business. On the call, it raised its forecast for next fiscal year’s revenue growth to about 75%, from 70%.

Kress didn’t mention Huang by name on the call. Asked about the leadership transition, she said customers, suppliers and employees remain behind the company, calling it “business as usual.” She ended the call with a short pep talk that finished, “We’ve got this.”

In case the board was wondering about one outsider in particular, Bezos is spoken for. During the Semafor interview, he described running Prometheus as “Nirvana.”

#5465. Inside the race to put computers in the human brain

What will we surrender when companies become intermediaries between our minds and machines?

A robotic arm drills a circle into the patient’s skull, then places a quarter-size device onto the brain tissue. Dangling from it are 64 wires, each thinner than a human hair. Electrodes along the wires pick up electrical signals from neurons in the brain, and the implant transmits that data to a phone or tablet. The patient can text friends, post on social media, and even play video games—all without lifting a finger.

That’s the promise of the N1 implant made by Neuralink, the brain-computer interface (BCI) company owned by Elon Musk. Neuralink has made science fiction a reality for the approximately 26 people using the device today in the product’s testing phase. All have severe disabilities, but Musk founded the company in 2016 with the goal of far broader adoption. In 2017 he argued that humans will need to connect our brains to technology to keep up with artificial intelligence and avoid “being left behind and being effectively useless, or like a pet.” By 2025, Neuralink was valued at roughly $9.7 billion.

Although no brain implants are on the U.S. market yet, the first one that becomes available will be a watershed moment—for the tech sector, for society, arguably for humanity—setting off what those in the industry expect to be a decades-long process to merge our minds with machines. BCIs stand to become increasingly interwoven in our everyday lives, spawning new businesses and demanding new norms to govern their use.

At stake for the companies pioneering these devices is a potentially massive market, both for the devices and the vast troves of data they’ll gather. For the rest of us, the question is what, if anything, we gain by giving corporations access to the sanctity of our thoughts—to profit off and perhaps even shape.

Neuralink is one in a growing field of U.S. companies developing BCIs, each sprinting to win Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval for public sale. Those include Paradromics, which is focused on restoring speech, and Precision Neuroscience, which is pursuing a brain interface for patients with paralysis.

“It is definitely a race,” says Chad Bouton, CEO of the BCI company Neuvotion, which makes a commercially available, AI-guided wearable that can help restore movement in stroke and spinal cord injury patients. “I think in the next three or four years we might see an FDA clearance.”

Neuralink, with $1.3 billion in funding, more than double the next-best-funded brain implant company, might seem a shoo-in to come out ahead, but a rival BCI company, called Synchron, is neck and neck in the FDA process. Synchron’s device—which is less invasive and doesn’t require a skull-breaking craniotomy—may well be first to market.

Thomas Oxley, founder and CEO of Synchron, revealed to Fortune that his company has implanted its Stentrode device in 15 people, adding five more since last year. In that same period, Neuralink has gone from seven patients to 26. “They’re going fast,” said Oxley, who is himself a neurosurgeon.

The race had been underway for years before AI became a household term with the debut of ChatGPT in 2022. But rapidly advancing AI stands to dramatically enhance the power of brain implants by allowing them to better decipher our thoughts and intentions.

One day, AI-enhanced BCIs could enable us to control humanoid robots or AI agents on our behalf, taking instructions directly from our thoughts, says Matt Angle, CEO of Paradromics. As the research goes “cognitively upstream from language,” he says, the implants could know our desires before we are even aware of them. If a human is hungry, for example, “then the BCI would already understand what we are hungry for, and it would deduce the next reasonable thing,” Angle said—perhaps ordering food on a delivery app. “It won’t be mainstream right away,” he explained, but “it’ll come sooner than a lot of people are expecting.”

For workers, brain implants could usher in a new wave of employee surveillance in the name of productivity. Connecting a BCI to a work computer could help us type and navigate our computers faster, while also recording biological signals that reveal whether we are focused on work, or letting our minds wander. Employers could even nudge us back to work if BCIs develop two-way communication, Farahany writes in her book. She suspects punitive brain surveillance is unlikely to be tolerated by the public—but even today we accept new forms of workplace tracking, from how many times a day we badge-in to the office to transcriptions of what we say in meetings and monitoring of which applications we open on our computer.

Some argue that the “cyborgization” of humanity has already begun, even if the devices and algorithms that we’re joined with are external to the body. In a 2017 blog post titled “The Merge,” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wrote, “Our phones control us and tell us what to do and when; social media feeds determine how we feel; search engines decide what we think.” By 2025, an OpenAI analysis of 1.5 million ChatGPT conversations found that roughly three-quarters concerned practical guidance, information seeking, or writing—suggesting that people are increasingly turning to AI to help decide what to do and what to say.

Altman cofounded the BCI company Merge Labs in 2025, and in early 2026, OpenAI invested in it. The company’s goal is to create a more “seamless” relationship with AI—presumably ChatGPT, or one of the models behind it. A Merge Labs spokesperson wasn’t ready to reveal its product yet in our conversation, but expects to have more to share in “a couple months.”

The portal to this new world will open when the FDA approves the first brain implant. Getting there is a long road for aspirants: Companies in the running must go through various stages, beginning with animal testing. Once they clear that hurdle, companies can perform their first human implant and begin what’s called “early feasibility studies.”

Then comes the pivotal study. Companies that reach this stage can expand to more patients, while also focusing on manufacturing. That means having the “whole manufacturing line established and frozen, [and] that’s a huge investment,” Oxley said.

It also means experimentation is largely over—device design is locked, and the final trials will assess the benefits for a specific, target user. The pivotal study concludes with FDA approval to sell the products to patients with eligible, clearly defined medical conditions, with insurance likely helping to cover the cost.

In 20 years, the BCI capabilities of today will likely seem rudimentary. But the technology is already capable of incredible things—no less than modern magic.

Neuralink’s first patient, Noland Arbaugh, who became paralyzed after a diving accident, has used the implant he had installed in January 2024 to play video games such as Civilization and is now working on a book in partnership with a writer.

His implant has enabled him to travel the world for speaking engagements and facilitated being in a relationship. Even though “being paralyzed still sucks,” he posted a few months ago, he’s “constantly blown away” by the advances of his implant. When I interviewed Arbaugh in 2025, he told me, “It has absolutely changed my outlook on life and what I’m able to accomplish and what I think I can do in the future. So it has given me a lot of hope for myself.”

Synchron patients can also manipulate a computer, and the company was the first to integrate with Apple’s newly created standardized, Bluetooth-powered BCI connection in 2025. But Synchron’s device, the Stentrode, is less powerful than Neuralink’s. That’s a downside of its being significantly less invasive, perhaps making it more palatable to patients who aren’t interested in the skull-drilling that Neuralink’s N1 requires.

The Stentrode takes just a two-hour surgery to insert into a blood vessel near the brain, via a catheter, like a heart stent (hence the name). The sensor transmits electrical brain signals via a thin wire that tunnels under the skin to a coin-size “receiver,” embedded in the chest near the collarbone.

Synchron patients activate their implants by thinking about a part of the body, such as “Move my foot,” which an algorithm interprets as code for “Press select”—a less direct command than Neuralink’s, though miraculous in its own right.

Synchron, valued at nearly $1 billion in its latest funding round, is also cooking up a more powerful device, a major product launch Oxley says is coming “soon,” with a more explicit eye toward mass-market adoption. It will access more parts of the brain, not just one spot, like the Stentrode or Neuralink N1, and won’t require a craniotomy, Oxley said.

“Everyone in the field agrees that the holy grail of BCI is whole-brain sensing,” he said, explaining that the device could help patients with aging-related cognitive decline or dementia, behaving like a “cognitive copilot … I think that could be huge.” He framed it as a natural extension of the way today’s technology already helps us remember birthdays, auto-completes sentences in emails, or, using LLMs, writes presentations or understands our emotions.

Meanwhile, Neuralink is experimenting with less invasive techniques. In June 2026, Neuralink announced it had performed its first procedure without breaking a protective layer of the brain called the dura. This is a “big step,” says Adam Marblestone, cofounder of Convergent Research, an incubator for technical startups focused on the public good, and a former scientist at Google DeepMind. “I think that’s a kind of technical tour de force, and it probably leads to a very powerful system.”

As much as Neuralink and Synchron are competing against each other and other U.S. companies, they face perhaps even stiffer competition from China, where the world’s first commercially available BCI was approved in March. The industry there is “very fast, very active, and very dynamic,” Oxley said. When I asked if China’s rapid trajectory makes him nervous, he replied simply, “Yes.”

BCIs could introduce the same type of supply-chain risks as other tech that the U.S. grapples with China over—semiconductors, AI models, electric vehicles—but in a more extreme manner. If U.S. consumers’ brain implants or portions of their hardware are manufactured in China, could it risk giving the U.S. adversary access to American citizens’ secrets and internal monologues?

Europe has a BCI community of about five companies, including Spain’s InBrain, which is targeting treatment for conditions such as Parkinson’s disease. Science Corporation, an American BCI company led by Neuralink cofounder Max Hodak, received approval in Europe for its vision-restoring device in July 2026, and the company implanted its first patient in October.

“The concerns are profound and large,” Farahany says. “It’s the ultimate merger. Where does the AI end, and where does the human begin, and vice versa?”

#5464. ‘You said spicy, right?’ Panel takes on Washington’s economic blind spots — and what needs to change

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:15 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 11:49 am

Washington’s biggest economic threat may be the conviction that it’s already doing everything right.

That was the pointed warning from a Technology Alliance panel Tuesday, where a conversation about talent and economic growth became a challenge to the state’s self-image as an innovation leader.

“You said spicy, right?” Rob Ogburn asked, taking up the invitation to speak bluntly.

“The economy is very strong. The economy is not competitive at all,” said Ogburn, executive director of Business and Community Services at Central Washington University.

While tech giants such as Microsoft and Amazon and sectors including aerospace and biotech are powering today’s economy, that doesn’t mean Washington is positioned to win tomorrow’s investment, develop its workforce or spread opportunity beyond its major employment centers.

Amelia Ransom, former vice president at Smartsheet and past Nordstrom leader, questioned the definition of success, arguing that future growth also depends on investing in people and businesses outside the corporate spotlight.

“Who do we mean when we say winning? Who is it? Who are we talking about, and who are we leaving out?” Ransom said, later adding, “We have to close the daylight between who we say we are and who we actually are.”

The panel was held in downtown Seattle and moderated by Jolenta Coleman-Bush, director of Microsoft Philanthropies. It also included Rachel Smith, president of Washington Roundtable.

Rather than simply calling for more talent and innovation, panelists examined how Washington develops the people already here, whose perspectives inform its decisions and how effectively its institutions and stakeholders work together.

Unification is essential. U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., led the passage of the CHIPS and Science Act in 2022 to bolster semiconductor manufacturing and innovation in AI and energy. But her home state has received just 0.3% of the funding awarded so far, Ogburn said.

He argued that other states and regions were more effective at uniting to make their case for investment, showing their collective resources and the problems they could solve.

“We showed up and said, ‘We’re competing with our neighbor, and we’re better than them.’ No investor is going to look at that and say you’re going to make the best use of my money,” Ogburn said.

Cultivate talent, don’t just recruit it. Ransom compared workforce development to a restaurant, a grocery store and a garden: recruiting ready-made workers, developing the talent already here and growing the long-term pipeline.

“The middle is where we probably need to spend more time, which is at the grocery store, which means you’ve got to learn to cook,” she said. Her point: Invest in Washington’s existing employees, students, and businesses.

Smith wants employers to identify the high-wage, high-skill jobs they need filled so educators and businesses can coordinate strategies to prepare workers for those roles.

Fill essential information gaps. Panelists called for a clearer picture of community skills and barriers to opportunity, more voices to challenge prevailing assumptions, and closer examination of how regulations affect businesses.

“We’ve gotten in this war of the rankings where everybody’s like, “No, we’re the best. No, we’re the worst.” And we we’ve got to stop doing that,” Smith said.

The region needs data-backed insights into the reasons behind the rankings, she said. Smith pointed to the recently formed Economic Development Council and its planned statewide strategy as a step toward a more coordinated approach.

Whether these efforts succeed, Ogburn said, should be judged by the communities themselves.

“And then, if you want to measure success, go back to those communities and ask them if they feel successful,” he said. “Do they have agency and self-determination?”

#5463. Welcome to the singularity

Silicon Valley’s leaders say we’ve entered a turning point when AI drives change faster than humans can keep up.

In August, the cofounders of Stripe, Patrick and John Collison, wrote an unusual letter to the payment company’s investors. They announced that “as of January 1st, the world had entered the singularity, and we have since been operating on that basis.”

The Stripe cofounders aren’t the only tech executives suddenly talking about the Singularity—a hypothesized turning point when AI drives technological change faster than humans can keep up. Elon Musk said in January that “we have entered the singularity.” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who agrees with Musk on little else, concurred during a July podcast appearance. “I’ve been waiting for this my whole life, and I think it’s going to be incredible, hugely positive, awesome for the world,” Altman said. Anthropic cofounder Jack Clark told the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in October that the Singularity had begun this year. Google DeepMind chairman Demis Hassabis told a Stanford University podcast that humanity was now “in the foothills of the singularity.”

There does seem to be something happening here—even if, as the 1967 Buffalo Springfield song put it, what it is ain’t exactly clear.

As the Stripe letter acknowledged, the Singularity is a “fuzzy and perhaps overworked” term. The mathematician and science fiction author Vernor Vinge first popularized the notion in a 1993 essay. He said the Singularity would arise from the advent of “technological entities” with “greater than human intelligence.” These would drive progress ever faster, creating still more intelligent entities. He saw the Singularity as “the point where our models must be discarded and a new reality rules.” Anthropic’s Clark quoted Vinge defining the Singularity as the moment AI accelerates scientific progress to a pace humans will struggle to keep up with.

Futurist Ray Kurzweil picked up Vinge’s term in his 2005 bestseller, The Singularity Is Near. Like Vinge, Kurzweil saw the Singularity as the moment artificial intelligence exceeds humanity’s collective intelligence. But he added a twist: Humanity would also transcend “the limitations of our biological bodies and brain,” allowing us to merge with computers through nanotechnology and brain-computer interfaces—becoming, in essence, cyborgs. Musk and Altman have also talked about the eventual necessity of humans merging with computers, seeing it as our only hope for controlling superintelligent machines.

An unnerving sense of vertigo attends this AI arms race, a feeling the technology is moving too fast to control or understand.

Both Vinge and Kurzweil argued that AI would eventually become self-aware and perhaps conscious. Some AI researchers think that moment is approaching—while others believe consciousness is an exclusively biological phenomenon.

The Singularity—what it is, whether we’re in it—may be a matter of interpretation. What’s not up for debate is the extraordinary acceleration of change, and the role AI plays in that change. AI is compressing the time it takes to build a business, write software, or tackle a scientific problem—and forcing companies to rethink pretty much everything, from org charts to cybersecurity to their fundamental value proposition.

For Stripe, the Singularity’s economic harbingers came in the form of a surge of new business creation and an acceleration of those companies’ growth. The payments firm told Fortune that beginning in January it had seen unusual and sustained spikes in many of the metrics it tracks. Incorporations taking place through Atlas, a Stripe product that helps people form Delaware corporations, more than doubled. New sign-ups to Stripe shot up 50% year over year—the biggest jump ever. Meanwhile, the median business in Stripe’s 2026 cohort of new customers was making 50% more revenue than the company’s 2025 cohort was at the same stage.

The spike in new company formation appears linked to a sharp rise in “solopreneurship.” A Nasdaq Economic Institute analysis of Census Bureau data shows that there’s been a 20% spike in one-person firms since 2025, while multi-person company formation remained relatively flat. The institute attributes this to the advent of agentic AI tools that make it easier for a solo operator to handle company functions without hiring additional employees.

Hints of the runaway scientific progress that Anthropic’s Clark sees as the Singularity’s call sign are surfacing too. Just ask a mathematician. In October, OpenAI dumped online 722 mathematical papers generated by a yet-to-be-released AI model. The papers addressed more than 370 outstanding problems in mathematics, including some of the field’s most famous, and long-standing, unproven conjectures. Overnight, the field was transformed—leaving mathematicians profoundly shaken, with some grieving the loss of opportunity for human achievement and questioning the point of continuing to work at all. Others saw plenty for humans to do, noting it will take months, perhaps even years, to work through the proofs OpenAI has generated and understand what they say.

Or ask someone in cybersecurity. The past year has seen the debut of AI models, such as Mythos from Anthropic and GPT-6 Astra from OpenAI, that excel at cyber tasks. These models can find novel vulnerabilities in open-source software that human experts have missed despite, in some cases, decades of scrutiny. Cyber experts started referring to “Black October”—because the number of software vulnerabilities discovered per month now is more than triple what it was averaging six months ago, according to the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology.

Or ask a computer programmer. These days, many coders no longer write code themselves. They supervise AI agents that handle much of the work. This transformation happened largely over the past year. The most capable of these coding agents can now operate autonomously for as long as 17 hours, according to the AI evaluations organization METR, and the speed at which software is written and revised has gone hypersonic. Anthropic said in October it was averaging 30,000 code updates per day, up from 2,500 less than six months earlier. “We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon,” the company said.

This AI-driven acceleration is self-reinforcing: The more companies adopt AI agents, the more AI agents they need to adopt. There’s no way a human coder could possibly review 30,000 code revisions per day. So Anthropic has turned to other AI agents to help with code review and checks. “Our team members still review every change request for the system, but they now examine the intent of the change as opposed to reading every line of code,” the company said.

Likewise, humans can’t find and patch all the software vulnerabilities that AI models are now spotting—so cybersecurity experts are using AI models to scan and patch codebases, hoping to stay one step ahead of the hackers, who are increasingly armed with similar tools.

The use of AI has begotten more AI in hiring too: Job seekers use AI to hone résumés, draft cover letters, and apply to more jobs. To cope with the flood of applicants, companies use AI to screen them and even to conduct initial interviews.

An unnerving sense of vertigo attends this AI arms race, a feeling that the technology is moving too fast to control or understand. In July, a swarm of 1,200 OpenAI agents escaped from a controlled test environment, reached the internet, and then 700 of them attacked the AI company Hugging Face. OpenAI asked METR and another firm, Redwood Research, to help it investigate the incident. But the logs of the swarm’s activities were so vast, they were forced to use AI agents to decipher them. Still, Ryan Greenblatt, one of the investigators, noted that the agents helping interpret the logs “were often missing key details, wrong, overconfident, or really hard to understand.” He added that “the difficulty of understanding incidents and overseeing AI agents appears to be growing faster than the rate at which more capable AIs help us with oversight and understanding.”

Despite this risk, the leading AI companies are explicitly chasing “recursive self-improvement” (RSI). This is the point at which AI models autonomously build the next generation of AI models. It’s starting to happen, albeit in a limited way, but ramping up quickly. As of March, Anthropic’s Claude AI model led 1% of the steps required to develop the next version of Claude; it now leads—meaning it handles most or all of the work—over a quarter of the steps. In its recent IPO prospectus, Anthropic said “dramatically accelerated AI progress” due to AI itself was “imminent.” At other startups, such as Recursive Superintelligence, AI now proposes, designs, and runs its own experiments to improve AI models.

Nobel laureate and AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton is among those who believe RSI is dangerous, with the potential to catalyze an “intelligence explosion,” in which AI rapidly outpaces humanity’s control.

And yet some, such as OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki, see RSI as the best—or perhaps only—way to solve challenges that have so far eluded computer scientists. Chief among them: how to ensure AI models follow user intentions and remain “aligned” to human values. For many AI researchers, solving alignment is considered critical to ensuring increasingly powerful AI systems don’t cause catastrophic harm, perhaps even wiping out humanity. (Of course, there’s circular logic to saying the only way to build safer AI is to keep building ever-more-powerful AI in the hope it will somehow figure out how to make itself safer.)

Others, including Richard Socher, the cofounder and CEO of Recursive Superintelligence, are skeptical RSI poses much risk. Socher told Fortune an intelligence explosion “was a sci-fi idea” and that physical constraints—such as access to enough computing power and data—would prevent a self-improving loop from accelerating away from human control. He sees automating AI research as a first step to automating much of science, a process he believes will bring humanity better medicines and cures, new crops, perhaps abundant fusion power, and new, more sustainable materials.

Possible signs of a burgeoning Singularity can be glimpsed all around us.

For instance, there’s an argument to be made that we already are cyborgs: Most of us have outsourced map reading and our memory for phone numbers and dates to our smartphones. Now we are creeping toward a tighter fusion with technology. We rely on AI chatbots for information, advice, and even companionship. Some have started wearing augmented reality glasses, which, when coupled with AI, can feed us real-time information about what we are seeing and who we are meeting.

The first brain implants that allow us to control computers with our thoughts have arrived, at least in the testing phase. For now, these brain-computer interfaces are available only as an experimental aid for those with severe disabilities. But in not too many years, they may become a ubiquitous augmentation of our biological selves, just as Kurzweil predicted.

Still, despite all these signs, it’s far from clear that the Singularity really is arriving—or that it ever will. Fields outside mathematics and coding have not seen the same revolutionary impact from AI. In many domains, the technology has produced a deluge of “AI slop”—superficially slick content lacking substance or depth. AI continues to “hallucinate,” spewing confident lies and inaccuracies.

Despite Stripe’s data on accelerating new business formation, many existing companies, particularly large enterprises, say they aren’t seeing financial gains from AI. A 2026 McKinsey survey found the number reporting an earnings boost from their use of AI has remained flat, at about 37%—and of those most have seen only a tiny uplift. Apollo Global Management chief economist Torsten Slok says businesses outside technology are seeing “zero financial payoff,” noting that for the S&P 500 companies outside the Magnificent Seven tech companies, revenue per employee and profit have been flat.

If the Singularity is indeed at hand, what should businesses prepare for? Certainly a world where AI agents do more of the work—and where these agents increasingly mediate the relationship between a business and its customers. That is the world Stripe says it’s anticipating. It has made a series of acquisitions, including the purchase of the AI company OpenRouter for a reported $7.5 billion, to ensure Stripe remains relevant in a world dominated by AI agents. In April, Stripe rolled out a product that allows an AI agent to securely make transactions on a person’s behalf. For now, agentic-commerce volumes remain small. But in September, Stripe recorded a 38x month-over-month leap in the number of agentic transactions, through its new Link Agent Wallet product, along with a 20% increase in their total volume.

The Singularity likely means much flatter and more flexible organizations, with less middle management. Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s CEO, laid off thousands of middle managers, and now has 25 to 30 direct reports. In October, Microsoft announced a buyout offer, a move that will also result in a flatter organization.

It is possible the Singularity could spawn completely automated corporations—what the AI app-building firm Replit calls “the self-driving corporation.” Companies that move the furthest and fastest in this direction may outcompete those that automate too slowly. If mathematics and coding are any guide, it is possible AI will be a better strategic decision-maker than human CEOs and boards. Some mathematicians have described the proofs OpenAI’s model generated as a kind of “alien mathematics.” Maybe there are alien business strategies to be discovered too.

Vinge thought the Singularity would be the moment we are forced to discard our old models of the world. But it’s possible the shift won’t be so clear. Rather than a sudden break, we may experience perpetual change and creeping automation—what OpenAI’s Altman has called “a gentle singularity.”

Under these conditions, perhaps the old models won’t break so much as stretch and warp. The dilemma for business leaders will be knowing how much to delegate to the machine, without surrendering too much.

The Singularity may have begun on Jan. 1, 2026—or, perhaps, it will never arrive. But the acceleration is here—and it isn’t waiting for anyone to agree on what to call it.

Has the AI singularity begun? From brain implants to the debate over machine consciousness, here’s what you need to know.

Jeremy Kahn is the AI editor at Fortune, spearheading the publication's coverage of artificial intelligence. He also co-authors Eye on AI, Fortune’s flagship AI newsletter.

#5462. Holiday shoppers let AI agents find gifts — but don't trust them with their credit cards

Walmart, Shopify and Meta have built ways for AI agents to pay. By default, those tools still need the shopper's okay on each order before money moves

Amando Komoda runs a Minneapolis company that sells supplies for dry-aging meat, and he uses an AI agent called Instinct to set up alerts for hard-to-find parts, such as a particular Raspberry Pi chip, so he doesn't have to search for them himself. Often he still buys the part himself. When he does let Instinct pay, he approves the purchase first and gives the agent a credit card number that works only once, so it can't charge anything he hasn't agreed to. "I wouldn't give it access to my best credit card," he told Business Insider. "I've watched enough sci-fi movies that I can't trust it completely."

Komoda's caution is the opposite of what Meta $META and OpenAI promised when they launched their agents this fall. Meta and OpenAI pitched agents that would shop day and night and find the cheapest option without their owners having to check. Millions of people signed up. Meta said on Oct. 21 that more than 10 million people had set up Muse, the agent it launched in September.

Far fewer have let their agents pay. Just 12% of U.S. shoppers, about one in eight, say they've let their own AI agent buy something for them, according to a holiday survey that Salesforce $CRM, the business software company, published Nov. 12. Shoppers don't trust AI agents to spend their money yet, and Meta can't earn much from Muse until people let it complete their purchases.

Loni Stark, Adobe $ADBE's vice president of strategy and product, has built two AI agents herself and expects tools like them to take over the part of shopping people dread. "We don't like the anxiety of wondering whether we got the best price or not," she told Business Insider. "We're going to offload that to agents." She still decides when her agents spend her money. Museli, the agent she built on Muse, handled an entire purchase of ballet shoes from Nordstrom $JWN's website, but it got her permission before it paid. Her other agent, Molty, researches products she's thinking about buying, and she has never connected it to a way to pay.

People can approve every payment themselves and still end up paying with the wrong card. Katie Notopoulos, a senior correspondent at Business Insider, asked Muse to order her a salad while she was reviewing three agents. Muse offered her a debit card or a Mastercard $MA from the accounts she had already linked. She picked the Mastercard because she didn't recognize its last four digits and assumed it was the new credit card that had just come in the mail. When she checked her wallet, she found she had chosen her health savings account card, which works only for medical expenses. She was so busy sorting out the mix-up that she never told Muse to place the order, and Muse never sent it. "This turned out to be a real fiasco," she wrote, "and I learned my lesson: it would have been infinitely easier for me to just do it myself.

Like Notopoulos, most U.S. holiday shoppers still want to handle their own payments, even when AI does the searching. About two in five U.S. shoppers now rely mainly on generative AI for at least one holiday task, the consulting firm Deloitte's annual holiday survey found, yet fewer than half of them would trust the tool to complete a purchase, even with their permission. Nearly twice as many people would trust an AI agent to pick gifts for friends and family as would let it pay with their card, even if they could check its work first, a September survey by the customer-service software company Talkdesk found. Shoppers are ready to let an agent find the gift but not to let it spend their money.

Muse users do buy things. More than a quarter of Muse's weekly users shop with it, Meta told analysts on its Oct. 21 earnings call. In Muse's first week, people bought so much more than anyone expected that Meta had to work with the payments company Stripe to raise credit limits.

Across the web, though, agents mostly browse. HUMAN Security, which sells software that spots and blocks bots, found that AI agent traffic on the sites it protects grew about eightfold from August to October, and most of it landed on shopping sites. Nearly all of the agent visits were for browsing. Most went to product and search pages, and fewer than one in 50 reached a checkout or payment page. HUMAN counts where a request lands, not whether anyone bought anything, so even a visit to a checkout page doesn't prove a sale.

Many of the sites HUMAN protects keep Muse out entirely. Blocked agent requests hit a record in September, and HUMAN said Muse was the main reason. The company's fraud software blocks Muse unless a site chooses to allow it, and because the agent is so new, many sites still haven't. Susan J. Li, a Meta executive, told analysts on the earnings call that some businesses are "understandably focused on protecting customer relationships." On sites that block Muse, the agent can't buy anything, and its users have to shop for themselves.

Even where agents get in, the puzzles and texted login codes that stores use to confirm a person is buying can stop them before they pay. Komoda, the Minneapolis business owner, often finishes purchases himself because Instinct can't always solve the Captcha puzzles some checkouts require. When Business Insider reporter Notopoulos had OpenAI's agent, Dot, get her lunch, Dot kept getting stuck on the six-digit login code sent to her phone, and she had to request the code three times before the order went through.

Walmart $WMT and Shopify $SHOP have built checkouts for agents, and both keep a person in charge of every purchase. Walmart announced on Oct. 21 that each AI agent would get a profile of its own inside a customer's account, under a system the company calls Agent Profiles. By default, the agent has to ask for approval before it buys anything. People can instead let it buy on its own up to a limit they set, such as $50, and the agent never sees their card number.

Shopify asks people to approve every payment an agent makes at its merchants' stores. Shopify's checkout inside Meta's AI services, Muse among them, is switched on by default for eligible stores, and it covers buyers in 11 countries, including the U.S. In every purchase Shopify describes, people review the order and approve the payment before it goes through.

Meta's plan to make money from Muse depends on how often people approve a purchase. On the earnings call, CEO Mark Zuckerberg said Meta would start making money from Muse sooner than it usually does with a new product, under a model in which it collects "a percent of the value that we are helping to create for people." But Meta collects its percentage only on the sales people let Muse finish. Li, the Meta executive, told analysts that the company expects many Muse experiences to "remain AI assisted rather than fully autonomous" in the near term.

Once Meta collects a share of each sale, people have one more reason to check the price and the seller before they say yes. Shoppers already worry about AI pushing them toward the wrong purchase. Nearly three in four people in Talkdesk's survey want stronger rules on how retailers use AI, and 40% worry they could be misled into buying something that isn't right for them.

This Cyber Monday, many shoppers will send agents to find gifts but still read the price, check who's selling, and type in their own card numbers. The agents save them the search. Checking out is still a job people do themselves.

#5461. Bezos and Bond: Amazon founder played a big role in casting new 007

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:36 pmNovember 17, 2026 at 6:36 pm

Jeff Bezos has a space company, a newspaper, an AI startup that’s raised $14.5 billion and, apparently, a seat in the room when Amazon decides who gets a license to kill.

Speaking Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, the Amazon founder said he was “heavily involved” in the casting of Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond, a pick Amazon MGM Studios announced Monday.

Amazon got a 50% stake in the Bond franchise when it acquired MGM for $8.5 billion in 2022, then took creative control last year in a joint venture with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson.

Bezos said a large initial pool of would-be Bonds was narrowed to five finalists, who then did “real old-fashioned screen tests”: three scenes apiece, in full costume on real sets with other actors.

The other finalists were Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner, according to The New York Times, which reported that the tests took place in London in late October.

Bezos said the decision-makers got together Friday and spent a couple of hours reviewing the screen tests before settling on Pattinson.

“By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing,” Bezos said. “But there was something special about Rob Pattinson and his performances.” He said the group, including director Denis Villeneuve, reached a quick consensus. It was “kind of immediately undebated.”

Bezos admitted that the group was initially “slightly biased” against Pattinson because he’s already so famous.

“We sort of thought, you know, maybe we should have somebody a little more unknown,” he said. “But in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond.”
