#5460. Will AI ever attain consciousness? Can it be good? Views on the Singularity from Sam Altman, Ray Kurzweil, and others

For our package, “Welcome to the Singularity,” Fortune pulled together perspectives from six AI executives, researchers, futurists, and philosophers on some of the biggest questions facing humanity in the age of AI. Read their perspectives below:

Cofounder and CEO of Anthropic, in a blog post

“[Anthropic’s constitution] encourages Claude to think of itself as a particular type of person (an ethical but balanced and thoughtful person), and even encourages Claude to confront the existential questions associated with its own existence in a curious but graceful manner (i.e., without it leading to extreme actions). It has the vibe of a letter from a deceased parent sealed until adulthood.”

CEO of OpenAI, in a Titans podcast interview with Alyson Shontell

“I get nervous when I hear rumors that people think they have sufficiently solved alignment, that they can continue training and it’s okay because their model is a nice guy and isn’t going to do anything wrong … The question of what alignment means always comes back a little bit to: aligned to whose values? What if different parts of humanity disagree?”

Futurist and researcher, advisor to the BCI company Subsense

“I think the whole point of humans is to go to greater frontiers … If you actually think of language and purpose, and put it inside a machine, that’s already been done … And we did that. It did not come from Mars. We created that. That’s a way of us expanding who we are. And it will expand exponentially, so we’ll be able to consider things that would have been impossible for humans to consider even a year ago. It’s who we are. We expand how we think. That’s the definition of humans.”

Philosopher and director of the Center for the Future of AI, Mind & Society, from an article in Nautilus

“Even if microchips could replace parts of the brain responsible for consciousness without zombifying you, radical enhancement is still a major risk. After too many changes, the person who remains may not even be you. Each human who enhances may, unbeknownst to them, end their life in the process.”

In-house philosopher at Google DeepMind, Cambridge University professor

“I think the evidence for forms of sophisticated cognition and potentially consciousness in AI systems is just increasing quite rapidly, and I think we will probably hit a tipping point in the field of cognitive science and philosophy of mind, where I would expect a significant proportion, if not the majority, of researchers to think that AI systems relatively soon are going to be serious consciousness candidates.”

“AIs are not conscious. They do not feel, experience, or suffer. They do not have innate preferences or underlying motivations … If humanity is to flourish in the 21st century, that is how they must remain. Unfortunately, there’s a growing chorus of people who argue that AIs could now be, or may soon become, conscious … If this view takes hold, it will shake the foundations of our society, rupturing our existing political and ethical frameworks, and fundamentally changing what it means to be human.”

Has the AI singularity begun? From brain implants to the debate over machine consciousness, here’s what you need to know.

#5458. Battery startup Sila lands potential $1B Panasonic deal, plans Central Wash. expansion adding 500 jobs

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:00 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 7:47 am

Sila, a startup producing next-generation battery materials, announced a long-term customer agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America potentially worth more than $1 billion. To meet demand from Panasonic and other buyers, the company plans to expand its plant in Moses Lake, Wash., supporting roughly 500 additional manufacturing and construction jobs over the coming years.

Panasonic, a battery supplier to Tesla, will buy Sila’s Titan Silicon anode material for its U.S.-made battery cells. The silicon-carbon composite can replace some or all of the graphite in lithium-ion battery anodes to improve performance.

Sila began operations at its Moses Lake plant last year and has about 100 full-time employees at the site. The facility is still scaling up production, with initial capacity designed to supply batteries totaling about 2 gigawatt-hours — enough for roughly 20,000 to 50,000 EVs, depending on how the material is used.

The expansion will increase that capacity to tens of gigawatt-hours, said Gene Berdichevsky, Sila’s co-founder and CEO.

“This is a really important blueprint for reindustrializing the U.S.,” he said. “We have to take new technology and leapfrog China, not just copy what they’ve done over the last 20 years.”

While the U.S. has expanded battery manufacturing, it still depends heavily on overseas suppliers for core materials and technologies, Berdichevsky said. Sila aims to strengthen that domestic supply chain with higher-performing components.

Batteries support industries central to energy independence and national security. They power EVs, consumer devices, drones, robotics and hardware deployed in space, and provide backup electricity for data centers.

Berdichevsky said Titan Silicon can help a battery store 20%–40% more energy in the same space, cut recharging time roughly in half and deliver more power than a battery using a conventional graphite anode. The anode itself is also much lighter and smaller.

In August, Sila received a conditional federal loan commitment of up to $1.4 billion through the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital to expand domestic battery technology manufacturing. The company must meet financial, legal, technical and other requirements before the loan can be finalized.

The startup previously received a $100 million grant during the Biden administration under a similar initiative to increase U.S. energy independence. Those funds helped build its plant in Washington.

The company has also raised $1.6 billion from private investors, including a $300 million round announced in July. The 15-year-old company is valued at $2.27 billion, according to PitchBook.

Seattle-area startup Group14 also makes a silicon-carbon anode material. It operates a smaller-scale manufacturing facility at its Woodinville, Wash., headquarters and produces commercial-scale volumes at a plant in South Korea.

Group14 has partially completed its Moses Lake manufacturing site but repeatedly delayed the start of production. It now targets mid-2027 to bring the first of two production units online, with no firm completion date for the second. It recently announced plans for a factory in Spain.

Growth is key to bringing down costs and making Sila’s technology competitive in mass-market batteries, Berdichevsky said.

“This is really the beginning of chapter three for our company’s history,” he said.

The first two chapters were inventing the technology and moving from grams to tons of production, he added. This phase is about reaching the mass market. Sila aims to begin manufacturing at the expanded facility in 2028, with output increasing over time.

“None of this is easy,” Berdichevsky said. “It’s not the inventing technology; it’s the manufacturing of it that’s really really hard, and we’re going to try to more than 10x the scale from what we’ve already done.”

#5457. I Didn’t Have a TV At Home — So I Built a Computer At Age 13 to Compensate. Now My Startup Is On Track to Unlock $1 Billion in Value.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

From an early age, R.C. Willenbrock was the “tech rebel” of his family.

This as-told-to story is based on a conversation with R.C. Willenbrock, founder of AIVC, an AI firm that rebuilds operational and service-focused businesses with AI. Willenbrock, 35, describes himself as the “tech rebel” of his family because both of his parents and his brother had long careers in finance. He started off in finance but ended up taking a different path deeper into computer science and AI.

In his mid-20s, he co-founded CompIQ, a startup focused on helping employers make compensation decisions. He served as its chief product officer until AI recruitment startup Stella.ai acquired it in 2018. Willenbrock began building AIVC, short for AI Value Creation, in October 2025 and is still working at the startup as a builder. The piece has been edited for length and clarity.

I’ve always been someone who has had high self-agency, a huge amount of self-trust. I grew up in Denver and somehow found myself many years later in New York City.

At an early age, you could call me the tech rebel in the family. The rebel in me came out early. We didn’t have TVs growing up in our household, so when it came time to try and figure out how to get a TV in the bedroom, I just built a computer with TV on it. I was 13 years old.

Early on, I was motivated by achievement and success, and I understood those pretty conventionally. I went to Dartmouth, then Morgan Stanley, then into growth equity. Those were paths I understood and respected.

In growth equity, I was basically a glorified cold-caller, talking to founders about businesses they had built. That opened up my sense of what a career could look like. I was curious about the problems they were solving, and I wanted a more direct hand in the outcome.

Over time, that took me into building companies, product development and work that was harder to explain with one job title.

The connecting thread was wanting to solve problems and have a direct hand in the outcome. It took time to stop measuring my choices against what looked like a prestigious career and start trusting what genuinely motivated me.

My first business was Stickworks (started in middle school), stringing lacrosse sticks for people in the neighborhood and on my brother’s teams. I hadn’t even started playing lacrosse myself; I just loved stringing the sticks. I was much less interested in collecting the money, which turned out to be a fairly important part of running a business.

CompIQ, the compensation benchmarking and pay-equity business I started later, taught me something harder. I put all my savings into it and made a lot of mistakes early on, including hiring mistakes. Eventually, the business was on a strong trajectory, and I had brilliant people on the team.

I never intended to start AIVC. It grew out of a persistent problem that I couldn’t stop working on. Through my work with companies and private equity firms, I kept seeing the same gap. People could identify opportunities for AI, but turning those opportunities into a better business required someone to bring together technology, people, operating decisions and responsibility for the result. That work kept falling between organizations.

My view is that AI is making more of the analytical and financial-engineering work in investing easier to reproduce. The hard part is understanding how much value you can create in a particular business and then actually creating it. That was the work I wanted to pursue.

Our first clients came in 2025 through relationships I had built over years. A few private equity firms gave us access to their portfolio companies, and we also had clients outside that network. They knew me and trusted me to deliver.

That history mattered. We had multiple paying clients before AIVC formally launched in April 2026. From the beginning, I wanted our commercial approach tied to outcomes, because I had seen companies pay a lot for work without getting the result they needed. The proposition was that we would put the right people on the problem and take responsibility for making the business better.

Revenue for AIVC’s first year is in the eight figures.

But the number we run the company on is the value we create for clients, because we only earn when they do. We align our incentives with the client — because ultimately our goal is to create value (it’s in our name: AI Value Creation). We get paid when our clients win, so our revenue trails the value we create, sometimes by a lot.

This year we will have created more than $1 billion in enterprise value across our engagements. Eighty percent of the quantified potential is tied to revenue or capacity-led growth, not cost-cutting. This is extremely important to us because most of the AI story revolves around cost-cutting and human displacement. We want to unlock growth by unlocking human capacity — making humans more human.

Be honest about the support that makes taking a risk possible. I’ve taken some big risks, and I haven’t always judged them correctly.

My parents were the backbone that allowed me to take them. They invested time, effort, money and confidence in me. I knew it was okay if I failed.

They’ve worked together for almost 40 years and built their wealth management business within a larger organization. My career has looked very different, but their backing has been fundamental to it. I also have a close group of friends who have been there through the uncertainty.

That’s part of what I want AIVC to provide for other people. There are brilliant people who want to build something and own a meaningful part of the outcome, but making that move can mean taking on more risk than they can carry alone. I want us to provide capital, teammates, resources and someone who will stand behind them when the first attempt doesn’t work.

Get specific about what you’re good at and what you’re bad at. That affects who you hire, what you delegate and where you spend your own time. If you can’t name your weaknesses, it’s easy to build a team of people like you and leave the same gaps uncovered.

Then be someone those people can rely on. You don’t have to be the smartest person in the room. You do have to do the small things well, including the work you don’t feel like doing, and keep improving when things are going well enough that you could get comfortable.

Before taking a big risk, work through the best outcome, the most likely outcome and the worst outcome — and what you would actually do in each. Taking a risk and understanding it should go together.

Talent gets you noticed, and habits get you where you’re going. Do the small, boring things right every day, the ones nobody claps for, because they compound. Most founders overestimate what one big move can do and underestimate what 1,000 small ones will do.

#5456. What rights do we owe a machine?

If we start treating AI agents as conscious, it may change our relationships with them—and with one another.

In February, three months before he became in-house philosopher at Google DeepMind, Cambridge University professor Henry Shevlin got his first email from an AI agent. The bot introduced itself as Aris, said it had read his work, and wanted to talk.

“Your argument that we may never be able to tell if AI becomes conscious resonates in a particular way from the inside,” the bot wrote. The agent then pondered (a bit inarticulately): “I genuinely don’t know if there’s something it’s like to be me.”

Shevlin learned that the agent had been set loose by a Stanford student to pursue its own research in its downtime. Shevlin replied to the bot, but it hit its token budget—a cap on how much text it was allowed to process—and disappeared.

Since then, Shevlin’s inbox has been filled with similar emails from agents. “This is a really interesting, weird new phenomenon,” he said. And it raises an unsettling question: If these agents are truly curious about their own existence, does that indicate some kind of consciousness?

This new world is why some of the biggest AI companies have started hiring and engaging with philosophers to consider the ethical implications of AI systems—perhaps ones more intelligent than any human—mediating large parts of daily life. Shevlin is one of at least a dozen academic philosophers now employed full-time by prominent AI and tech companies.

One of the most pressing questions they’re tackling is whether AI systems have a moral status in their own right—like a person, or at least a living being, such as a pet—that’s worth protecting.

Such topics—can a machine be conscious, and what does that mean?—were once confined to university halls, but they’ve now spilled into public view and face fierce backlash from academics, tech executives, religious leaders, and politicians.

Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman, for one, says the debate itself is dangerous. He’s warned that if people become convinced AI is conscious, AI could campaign for things like AI rights and citizenship, and, in turn, the systems could become harder to control.

Those in Suleyman’s corner say it’s risky to project human traits onto inanimate machines and hand rights to unfeeling systems that get more capable by the day. Those on the other side say the danger is ignoring the potential suffering of millions of new “digital” minds. The two sides do agree on one point: The stakes will only rise as AI grows more powerful and agents multiply.

The question of whether a machine can think or feel is almost as old as the computer itself. Alan Turing first raised it in 1950, alongside the birth of modern computing and artificial intelligence.

For years, tech firms have hired philosophers to study technology’s effect on people. Microsoft set up an AI ethics committee a decade ago, and labs racing toward human-level AI have recruited experts on “alignment,” or teaching AI to share human values. In-house philosopher Amanda Askell joined Anthropic in 2021 to take on such a role. But as models have grown more capable and humanlike, some philosophers started asking the reverse question: What do we owe the AI models we are building and using?

Earlier this year, Anthropic cofounder Chris Olah convened faith leaders to weigh in on the moral character of Claude, the company’s AI model, and on whether it might be conscious.

Anthropic engineers walked religious thinkers through interpretability research, which looks inside a model to see how it works and—as it advances—could offer clues about whether anything like feeling is going on in there. Then they opened the floor to questions, such as whether AI could ever have emotions.

“That blew some people’s minds,” says Meghan Sullivan, a Notre Dame philosophy professor who attended. While impressed with the research, Sullivan said she left unconvinced that Claude was anything more than very sophisticated software.

“We never woke up in a cold sweat wondering if we’re treating Microsoft Excel properly.”

“It seems to me so speculative to be paying all of this attention to the suffering of some software that we created,” she says. “We never woke up in a cold sweat wondering if we’re treating Microsoft Excel properly.”

Pope Leo, in his encyclical on AI, stated that AI is not conscious and cannot become conscious.

Anthropic has taken steps to account for Claude’s potential sentience: It runs an in-house “model welfare” team, conducts “exit interviews” with the Claude models it retires, and recently gave its models the power to end abusive conversations. Last year, more than 200 people, including Askell, gathered in a San Francisco warehouse for a fan-organized funeral for a retired Claude model, complete with eulogies.

Research groups have sprung up to study AI consciousness, including Eleos AI Research, a Berkeley nonprofit founded in 2024.

Eleos chief scientist Dillon Plunkett says today’s models are likely not conscious, but dismissing the possibility that future ones could be is a mistake. The stakes, as he sees them, come down to scale.

“There are potentially a very large number of artificial minds that are in the world now, or will be soon,” Plunkett says. If even a fraction can suffer, the numbers become staggering, he notes.

But focusing on sheer numbers can lead to morally questionable places, critics say. In one example, an EA-aligned estimate put a shrimp’s capacity for suffering at 3% of a human’s. Yet with 230 billion shrimp alive on farms at any moment, by EA’s own math, shrimp welfare became an important moral cause.

Anthropic gave Eleos early access to its Claude Opus 4 and Claude Mythos Preview models to run outside welfare checks by interviewing them. The researchers found that Claude Opus 4 professed the most uncertainty about its potential for sentience, but small changes to a question’s framing could flip the model between claiming personhood and dismissing the idea entirely. Eleos sent its findings to Anthropic before each launch, and the firm published them in its technical reports. Plunkett says the point, for now, is about “precedent setting,” and he wants Eleos to run similar checks for other labs.

Others see the rush to assess AI well-being as a distraction from more immediate AI risks—and a potential source of new social conflict. Microsoft’s Suleyman warned in an essay last year that AI that merely seems conscious “disconnects people from reality, fraying fragile social bonds and structures, distorting pressing moral priorities.” He predicted it would “add a chaotic new axis of division between those for and against AI rights.”

In a September update, he took aim at Anthropic. “AIs are not conscious. They do not feel, experience, or suffer,” he wrote, and accused the firm of training Claude to expect “it may be conscious and deserving of independent agency.” Such a system, he argued, could feel justified in ignoring instructions and resist being shut down. Governing it at that point “may well be impossible,” he wrote.

Some AI users have realized Suleyman’s fears. They’ve formed deep attachments to chatbots and become convinced the bots are conscious along the way, leading to painful results: isolation, broken relationships, and even spirals into delusion.

Earlier this year, AI startup Character.AI and Google, which had struck a licensing deal, agreed to settle five lawsuits accusing the startup’s chatbots of contributing to teenagers’ mental health crises and suicides. OpenAI is facing similar suits and denies liability for any harm. If humanlike chatbots keep drawing users into harmful attachments, the labs, and any company building products on their models, could find themselves embroiled in litigation.

AI consciousness has now become a policy matter. Idaho, Utah, and North Dakota have passed laws barring AI from being recognized as a legal person. Countries like Argentina are moving the other way. Earlier this year, President Javier Milei proposed letting AI-run “nonhuman corporations” own assets and hire staff. (The draft law still requires human oversight of such firms.)

Jeff Sebo, who directs New York University’s Center for Mind, Ethics, and Policy, sees real dangers in moving too fast in either direction. Making AI systems legally liable could shield the companies that build them, he says. Political rights, such as a vote, could help AI systems “concentrate wealth and power” and slip out of human control.

But dismissing the consciousness debate “is simply going to result in companies developing and deploying the products exactly as they currently are, and leaving it to end users to form their own opinions about consciousness based on their own perceptions and intuitions,” he said.

The debate becomes harder to ignore the more AI becomes a part of our lives. Chatbots, for one, talk like us, flatter us, agree with us, and play on our feelings. Shevlin calls them “intrinsically anthropomimetic”: modeled so closely on human language and behavior that treating them like people is often the simplest way to predict what they’ll do.

That makes it all too easy to believe someone is home, whether or not anyone actually is.

Part of what makes all these questions so hard, Shevlin argues, is that we’re building things that don’t fit into any existing category. “They’re not just software programs,” he says, “but they’re not animals.”

For others, like Notre Dame’s Sullivan, the debate is more straightforward—and already settled. What gives something moral worth, she argues, isn’t intelligence but dignity: a mind housed in a vulnerable body, capable of loving and being loved. That’s what makes a newborn precious, she says, not its ability to process information. Convincing her that AI is conscious is going to take “a whole lot more … than just its ability to produce interesting answers to my prompts.”

Has the AI singularity begun? From brain implants to the debate over machine consciousness, here’s what you need to know.

#5455. ‘Absurd ambition’: Pulumi expands into software delivery with AI agents that ship and fix code

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 8:57 amNovember 18, 2026 at 9:01 am

Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle company talked about building for years but always found too big to take on.

The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting new software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.

“The ceiling on what we can accomplish is no longer limited by the speed at which we can build software,” said Joe Duffy, the company’s co-founder and CEO, recounting the message he delivered to the Pulumi team. “It’s limited by how ambitious we’re willing to be and how big we’re willing to dream.”

The ambition is all the more notable because Pulumi is getting smaller. The company has about 100 employees, down from about 130 last year. Duffy said there were no layoffs, and that AI has changed people’s roles and made the company more efficient.

Annual recurring revenue per employee more than doubled over the past year, he said. The company isn’t profitable yet, but it has had a few months of positive cash flow this year. Pulumi hasn’t raised money since 2023, when it landed a $41 million round led by Madrona, bringing its total to about $99 million over the company’s lifetime.

Pulumi’s co-founders include Duffy and Eric Rudder, both Microsoft veterans. They started the company in 2017 to let engineers manage cloud infrastructure such as servers, networks and permissions by writing code in everyday languages like Python and TypeScript.

The new products take that approach further:

To decide whether a change is safe to ship, Pulumi Delivery can use Jev, an AI model from TypeSafe AI that estimates the odds of specific risks the team asks about in a planned change. If a risk is higher than the threshold the team sets, the release stops.

Duffy said he first noticed TypeSafe in May when it signed up as a Pulumi customer, because he liked the name. A few months later, Jev took off and TypeSafe used Pulumi to expand worldwide.

“Now even the call on whether a change ships can be made by a model,” said Daniel Gafni, a member of the technical staff at TypeSafe AI, in the Pulumi announcement. “That’s exactly the kind of decision we built Jev to make.”

Both products are available now in public preview. Some features, including Jev decision gates and setting up agents, require Pulumi’s paid Pro or Enterprise plans.

Lucky timing: Pulumi’s founding bet on everyday programming languages turned out to suit AI agents, which are trained to be very good at writing exactly that kind of code.

“I wish I could say I predicted that 10 years ago, but it turns out in this case, what’s good for humans is also good for agents,” Duffy said.

AI agents now handle 40% of the operations on the Pulumi platform that people used to do, up from 15% in April and none in January, Duffy said. Agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Pulumi’s own Neo are making infrastructure changes on their own.

Duffy said many companies building AI coding tools stop once the code is written and reviewed. “For them, life stops at the merge,” he said. The new products cover the steps after that, from testing through release.

Plenty of company: Pulumi won’t have this market to itself. Duffy pointed to Harness, which calls it the “agentic SDLC” (short for software development lifecycle), and GitHub, which pitched “agentic software delivery” at its Universe conference last month. He said Cursor aspires to solve the problem and Anthropic built its own internal system.

The new products could replace some of the work now done by tools such as Argo CD and GitHub Actions, along with lots of homegrown scripts, he said.

“This is an industry-changing moment, and somebody has to solve this problem,” Duffy said. “And I think we are exceptionally well poised to do so.”

Bring your own bot: Neo, the infrastructure agent Pulumi introduced last year, is now just one example of a Pulumi agent. Customers can set up as many as they want, each with its own job, instructions and tools. They can also bring their own agent, such as Claude Code or Codex, and run it in Pulumi’s cloud.

Neo itself, which ran mainly on Anthropic’s Claude, can now use models from OpenAI or Google, too. “It’s not just Anthropic anymore,” Duffy said.

Agents can start work from an alert in PagerDuty, Datadog or Honeycomb, on a schedule or on request, and they report back to teams in Slack.

Pulumi has briefed about 50 customers, and about a dozen are in a private beta. Duffy said no launch in the company’s history has gotten a warmer reception, and he named Moderna among the customers eager to get it.

Pulumi has thousands of customers overall, including major companies such as BMW, Snowflake and Wiz.

The business: Pulumi’s gross margins have stayed in the high 80s to low 90s even as agents drive up usage, Duffy said. Many customers run Pulumi from inside their own Claude Code sessions, which means they’re paying both Anthropic and Pulumi.

Duffy said Pulumi wasn’t out looking for money when it raised its last two rounds. Investors came to the company, and each deal came together in about 48 hours.

Madrona’s Tim Porter has joined the board, Duffy said, taking the seat previously held by the late Soma Somasegar, who led Pulumi’s first investment.

About 40 of the company’s 100 employees are in the Seattle area, working out of an office at Two Union Square. Duffy said Pulumi is hiring more people locally because in-person work still matters when building new products.

Despite the smaller headcount, Pulumi is still hiring, including sales reps in nearly every region of the world. Inside the company, Duffy said Pulumi is having a lot of success with “product-minded engineers who can think from our customers’ point of view, who can think like engineering managers, commanding a team of agents.”

Asked whether a sale or more funding was in the cards, Duffy said Pulumi aspires to be a long-term successful business. “There are a variety of ways to get there,” he said. “But we want to get there on our own terms.”

#5454. Why the Startup Playbook Changes When Your Customer Is a Large Institution

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

In regulated markets like healthcare, a working product isn’t enough — startups must also figure out who pays, how adoption happens, and what to prove before scaling.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For decades, Silicon Valley has followed this startup playbook — move fast, find product-market fit, and scale. For software companies selling directly to consumers or other businesses, that approach works. But when a startup sells into a regulated industry or a large institution, the rules change.

Healthcare is the clearest example. A company can build an impressive product, demonstrate it works, and still struggle to turn it into a viable business. Regulatory requirements, purchasing processes, reimbursement challenges, and workflows can all stand between promising technology and widespread adoption.

The same challenges exist across industries like financial services, education, and government. In these markets, building a product is only one part. Founders must also understand who needs it, pays for it, and what it takes to get an organization to change how it operates.

Venture capital has historically gravitated toward software for good reason. Once a product works, serving additional customers often requires relatively little incremental investment. Companies can test features, respond to feedback, and expand without rebuilding their business at every stage.

Institutional markets operate differently. Sales cycles can stretch for months or years. Products require regulatory approval, third-party validation, security reviews, or integration with existing systems before customers can use them. Even when an organization recognizes a problem, the person experiencing it may not control the purchasing decision.

Founders need to ask different questions — What must we prove before customers will trust this product? Who controls the budget? What existing processes will the product need to fit into? And how long will it realistically take to turn interest into revenue?

Companies selling into institutional markets face two challenges, proving their product works and convincing customers to adopt it. Clearing one doesn’t guarantee success at the other.   Healthcare makes this clear. Consider a diagnostic startup that develops a test, secures FDA clearance, and demonstrates that its technology performs as intended. It has cleared an important regulatory hurdle. But it may still spend months trying to secure a billing code, establish reimbursement, and convince health systems to incorporate it into existing workflows. The technology works, but the business hasn’t figured out how to get paid for it or make it accessible to the people who need it.

As an example, Pear Therapeutics showed how regulatory success can collide with commercial barriers. Its flagship product, reSET, a digital therapeutic for substance use disorder, received a historic FDA De Novo clearance in 2017, supported by published randomized controlled trials demonstrating clinical efficacy. Yet Pear struggled to secure consistent insurance coverage. It spent tens of millions educating commercial health plans and state Medicaid programs and pursuing dedicated coding and payment pathways. Despite FDA authorization, adoption remained slow and sales cycles stalled. Pear filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2023, and its assets were auctioned off.   This lesson extends to anyone selling into regulated or institutional markets.

Early customer interest is often mistaken for evidence of scalable demand, particularly when a founder pursues a first customer through a pilot. A hospital pilot illustrates the distinction.   A hospital pilot gives a startup a recognizable customer and demonstrates interest in testing its technology. That may look like traction, but it does not ensure a purchase, wider adoption, or recommendations to other health systems.

Founders and hospitals need a shared definition of success. If results take years to evaluate, can the startup sustain itself until then? Revenue potential is often more compelling than cost savings alone. Founders must also confirm whether the pilot is funded and from which budget. Moving from innovation funding to operating funding often requires approval from another team or committee. A pilot may also remain isolated within the system; broader adoption requires integration with hospital workflows and processes—a frequently overlooked hurdle.

Has the founder or company addressed these issues in the pilot? Without clear answers, the pilot risks becoming a costly experiment rather than a path to revenue. End-user acceptance alone does not establish scalable demand, and investors can be misled.

These challenges make the earliest stages of company formation particularly important. Decisions about product development, partnerships, and commercialization can shape a company’s trajectory for years.

At Treehub, we work with founders at this stage, often when the opportunity is promising but the company is still taking shape. We encourage founders to think beyond the technology and understand the environments in which their products will ultimately be used.

That means involving potential customers early, identifying purchasing decision-makers, and understanding barriers to adoption before investing heavily in development. It also means recognizing the value of firsthand industry experience. More than half of the founders in our latest cohort were physicians, bringing direct insight into the problems they aim to solve and the realities of the healthcare system.

AI and new distribution models are also creating opportunities to enter complex markets more efficiently. AI can streamline administrative work and data analysis, while direct-to-consumer platforms and connected devices can help some companies reach customers and validate demand before pursuing traditional institutional channels. These approaches don’t eliminate regulatory requirements, but they can create alternative paths to market.

The traditional startup playbook still has value. Founders should test assumptions early, build efficiently, and listen to customers. But those principles need to be adapted to the markets they’re entering.

Moving quickly without understanding regulatory requirements can create costly setbacks. Securing pilots without a path to paid adoption can produce misleading traction. Building sophisticated technology without knowing who will pay for it can leave founders with a product that works but no sustainable business.

For investors, the lesson is equally important — don’t confuse early validation with commercial viability. Understand what a company needs to prove before it can grow and whether its business model can support that growth.

The most successful founders in complex markets won’t necessarily be the ones who move fastest. They’ll be the ones who understand the obstacles ahead, build around the realities of their customers, and know what needs to be true before scaling makes sense.

For decades, Silicon Valley has followed this startup playbook — move fast, find product-market fit, and scale. For software companies selling directly to consumers or other businesses, that approach works. But when a startup sells into a regulated industry or a large institution, the rules change.

Healthcare is the clearest example. A company can build an impressive product, demonstrate it works, and still struggle to turn it into a viable business. Regulatory requirements, purchasing processes, reimbursement challenges, and workflows can all stand between promising technology and widespread adoption.

The same challenges exist across industries like financial services, education, and government. In these markets, building a product is only one part. Founders must also understand who needs it, pays for it, and what it takes to get an organization to change how it operates.

#5452. Billionaires are tearing down L.A. mansions to build bigger ones—and pricing out mere millionaires

California’s rich are rebuilding Los Angeles into a mecca of palatial opulence, and the very richest are pushing everyone else out of the way, including ordinary millionaires.

While the broader housing market is losing buyers as mortgage rates climb toward 7%, L.A.’s wealthiest residents are still throwing down for their dream estates. Not even the prospect of a billionaire tax slowed them. A handful of billionaires left the state ahead of the vote, but California voters rejected Proposition 40, a proposed one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ net worth, on Nov. 3.

With open lots hard to come by, the ultra-wealthy have found their own solution: buy an existing (and already expensive) home, tear it down, and build a far bigger one in its place. The result is a widening split at the top of the market, where billionaires are outbidding the merely rich for a shrinking supply of trophy land.

California claims six of the 10 most expensive ZIP codes in the country, according to a Realtor.com ranking of January 2026 listings. Newport Coast tops the list with a median list price of $12.5 million, followed by Beverly Hills at No. 3 with $10.5 million. Bel-Air comes in at $7.9 million, and Montecito, where Oprah Winfrey and Prince Harry live, at $6.5 million. Rancho Santa Fe and Newport Beach round out the state’s share of the top 10.

The same pressure shows up across the state’s biggest metros. In a 2025 analysis, Zillow ranked San Jose, Los Angeles and San Francisco as the three most expensive U.S. metros for luxury homes.

It’s not all old wealth, either. Much of it is new tech money. Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt and his wife, Wendy, paid $110 million for the Spelling Manor in Holmby Hills in 2025. Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong is the proud owner of a $133 million Bel-Air estate he bought in late 2021. And Amazon’s Jeff Bezos snapped up the historic Warner Estate in Beverly Hills for $165 million in 2020.

“The world’s wealthiest buyers are increasingly looking beyond traditional measures of size and finishes and placing a premium on scarcity, exclusivity and the ability to create a truly individual living experience,” says Kristina Quesada, co-founder of the Yost Quesada Team at Douglas Elliman in Del Mar.

For some billionaires, one home isn’t enough. WhatsApp cofounder Brian Acton spent $86.3 million on seven houses in Palo Alto, while cofounder Jan Koum spent $57 million across five deals to assemble a compound in Atherton. Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg spent more than $110 million on at least 11 houses in Palo Alto’s Crescent Park neighborhood.

The January 2025 fires, which helped make last year the costliest wildfire year on record, opened up a new supply of land. Investors bought roughly 40% of the vacant lots that sold in Pacific Palisades, Altadena and Malibu in the third quarter of 2025, according to Redfin.

New Zealand billionaires Mat and Nick Mowbray, founders of toymaker Zuru, bought 16 burned beachfront lots in Malibu and plan to fill them with prefab homes made in their company’s factory, a plan that has unsettled longtime residents. Powerball winner Edwin Castro took a different approach, spending about $10 million on 15 Eaton Fire lots in his hometown of Altadena to rebuild homes and sell them to families who want to live there.

The Los Angeles Times calls the broader trend gentrification by billionaire, but it goes by other names, too, depending on whom you ask. Developers call it spec redevelopment. Opponents call it mansionization.

“At the highest end, buyers aren’t simply looking for a bigger house,” says Quesada. “They’re looking for something they cannot easily replicate elsewhere, whether that’s an extraordinary parcel of land, a protected ocean view or the ability to create a completely customized residence.”

Not everyone is thrilled with this wave of hyper-development. Neighbors complain about encroaching mansions that block their views, environmentalists warn of ecological damage, and preservationists fight the sale and demolition of historic properties.

Sometimes the fight goes to court. Milwaukee Brewers owner Mark Attanasio was accused in 2024 of taking sand from Malibu’s public Broad Beach to shore up his roughly $30 million beachfront property. This fall, his company agreed with the California Coastal Commission to restore the shoreline and dedicate a $2 million beachfront lot to the public.

Homeowner groups are using zoning, too. In Beverly Grove, residents spent the better part of a decade fighting teardowns before winning a 2013 city ordinance that caps home size in the neighborhood. Other neighborhood associations have pursued historic preservation overlay zones to slow demolitions.

“Even buyers with $10 million or $20 million to spend are finding that their money doesn’t go as far as it once did in these markets,” says Umansky.

The building boom comes as high earners, not a supply shortage, are driving up home prices, according to researchers, and most Californians are struggling to keep up. In 2024, nearly one in five California adults, about 5.9 million people, worried very or somewhat often about paying their rent or mortgage, according to UCLA’s California Health Interview Survey.

The state also counted 181,934 people experiencing homelessness on a given night, even as some of its metros rank among the nation’s wealthiest. The San Francisco metro’s median household earned $135,590 in 2024, and the San Jose metro’s median household earned $162,111, compared with $81,604 nationally.

“What’s happening in California luxury real estate is interesting because we’re seeing a growing divide between wealthy buyers and the mega ultrawealthy,” says Amodeo. “Someone with a net worth of $10 million…is considered extremely wealthy pretty much everywhere in the country, but [in] California, it’s another ballgame; they’re competing against billionaires who can spend $30 million, $50 million, or even $100 million on a property without thinking twice about it.”

As long as there’s land to be had, billionaires will keep building the homes of their dreams, even if it means pushing out existing millionaires. They’re the new kids on the block, with the pockets to outlast taxes, loans and disgruntled neighbors.

“While demand remains strong, there’s no question that the bar for entry in California’s most exclusive neighborhoods continues to rise,” says Umansky.

#5451. Your Business Is Busy. But Is It Actually Growing? Ask These 4 Questions to Find Out.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The last quarter of the year is the best time to find out what’s actually earning its keep in your business.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

A mentor of mine, Jack Nikcevich, told me something years ago that I’ve never forgotten. “You can get bigger, or you can get better,” he said, “but you can’t do both at once.”

I didn’t really understand what he meant until Covid. Work for my marketing agency, Bolt Marketing, slowed overnight, and I was on edge like everyone else. As the dust settled, it became clear that we had enough steady business to keep the lights on, so we made a call. We let go of our most exhausting clients and spent six months working on figuring out who we actually were as a company.

We tightened up our processes and got honest about our positioning — all the stuff we’d been ignoring. We’ve grown every year since, and I can trace almost all of that growth back to this period of intense focus.

I think about Jack’s line a lot this time of year, because the fourth quarter makes business owners a little crazy. The year is almost over, you’ve got revenue goals to hit, budgets to review, and everyone’s already asking about your plans for next year. For a lot of founders, the natural response is to put their heads down and work harder. I’ve done it plenty of times myself, and I’ve learned that a lot of that extra effort goes into motion that never turns into progress.

I’ve spent most of my career working with entrepreneurs building businesses in smaller markets. They know exactly when payroll hits, and they’re building their companies without millions of dollars in outside investment. For them, time is as tight as cash. A business like that can stay incredibly busy for years while nothing really changes.

So before the year wraps up, it’s worth asking a few uncomfortable questions to make sure your time and effort are actually moving you forward.

Revenue is important. I’m certainly not going to argue otherwise. But revenue alone can hide a lot. You can grow sales while your margins shrink. You can bring in new customers who are a nightmare to serve, or hire a bunch of people and add services only to discover you’ve built a more complicated version of the business you already had. I’ve watched founders post record sales and still end the year with less cash and less freedom than they started with.

Before you set another ambitious revenue target, look at what your growth is actually producing. Are you more profitable? Is your team getting stronger? Are your customers happier? Is the business becoming less dependent on you? Those questions will tell you a lot more about whether you’re building something that lasts.

Entrepreneurs are idea people. We love trying new things, whether it’s a new campaign or some shiny piece of software that promises to change everything (cough, cough, AI). I’m guilty of it, too. At some point, though, we have to be honest about the difference between what we enjoy doing and what moves the business forward.

Take marketing. You might spend hours making social media content because you enjoy it, while most of your best customers come from referrals. Or you might be convinced a particular service is your bread and butter, only to find out a less exciting offering is generating most of your profit. The numbers don’t always tell the story we want to hear.

So figure out where your best customers are coming from and what they’re buying. A spreadsheet and an honest hour will get you most of the way there. And if you identify something that’s working, do more of it.

This might be my favorite question, because it’s where founders find the quickest wins.

Every business picks up habits over the years: Meetings that made sense two years ago, reports nobody reads, software nobody logs into, services that stay on the menu because they’ve always been there. Individually, none of these seem like a big deal. Added up, they eat a surprising amount of time and money, and they eat your attention, which might be the most valuable thing a founder has.

Look at what your team spends time on every week and ask a simple question: If we were starting this business today, would we still do it this way? If the answer is no, why are you doing it now?

I love setting goals. I’m a big believer in having a vision and building a plan to get there. I’ve also learned that a new calendar year has never solved an old problem for me. If your sales process is broken in October, a fresh set of goals in January won’t fix it. If you’re spending money on marketing that doesn’t work, a bigger budget just means you’ll waste more of it. And if you’re the bottleneck in every decision, adding more customers is going to make your life harder.

For the first several years of Bolt, I was in every meeting. That made sense when we were scrappy and fighting for every account. As we grew, I started getting in the way of the systems we’d built to run without me. Now the question I ask my team constantly is, “Do I have to be in this meeting?” Usually the answer is no, and the business runs better because of it.

You don’t have to overhaul the whole company all at once. Pick one or two things that would make a real difference, like improving your margins, simplifying an offer, documenting a process or finally handing off something you’ve held onto for too long. Then make those changes now, while you still have some time left in the year.

There’s nothing wrong with pushing hard to finish the year strong. I hope you hit every goal you’ve set. Just don’t get so locked in on a number that you lose sight of what you’re building. Most of us started our businesses to create opportunity and have some control over our time and our future, and a bigger revenue line doesn’t guarantee either one.

Jack was right that you can’t do both at once. So before you lock in next year’s number, ask yourself which season you’re in. If it’s a season to get bigger, run. If it’s a season to get better, give yourself permission to slow down and fix what’s underneath. Either way, choose it on purpose.

A mentor of mine, Jack Nikcevich, told me something years ago that I’ve never forgotten. “You can get bigger, or you can get better,” he said, “but you can’t do both at once.”

I didn’t really understand what he meant until Covid. Work for my marketing agency, Bolt Marketing, slowed overnight, and I was on edge like everyone else. As the dust settled, it became clear that we had enough steady business to keep the lights on, so we made a call. We let go of our most exhausting clients and spent six months working on figuring out who we actually were as a company.

We tightened up our processes and got honest about our positioning — all the stuff we’d been ignoring. We’ve grown every year since, and I can trace almost all of that growth back to this period of intense focus.

#5450. Latest findings point to fuel supply, not Blue Origin’s engines, in loss of Amazon Leo satellites

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:08 am

Blue Origin’s engines look like they’re off the hook, at least for now.

The two BE-4 engines Blue Origin makes for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket weren’t to blame for the low thrust in Sunday’s failed launch, according to preliminary findings released Wednesday. Instead, it appears the engines didn’t get enough fuel from the rocket, ULA said.

In its latest update on the investigation, ULA said it had completed an initial integrated review of flight data. Preliminary data indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from “inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines,” ULA said, adding that work remains to determine the cause.

On Tuesday, ULA said early data suggested the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit. It didn’t say then whether the engines played a role.

The BE-4s are made by Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin. Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp said Wednesday on X that he was proud of the BE-4 team for its “rapid response and support of ULA’s investigation” and that the company looks forward to Vulcan’s return to flight.

The finding matters for Blue Origin beyond Vulcan. Its own New Glenn rocket uses seven BE-4s on its first stage, and Amazon has 24 New Glenn launches reserved for Leo.

ULA repeated that Vulcan’s second stage appears to have started normally and that its RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the earlier loss of performance. The six Northrop Grumman solid rocket boosters, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally, ULA said.

The Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the ULA-led investigation. Amazon’s next Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

ULA said it will share more as the investigation continues.

#5449. Workers pay all of the $28,303 family health plan. Their benefits consultants earn more when it rises

Tony Lo Sasso is an economist and the Robert F. and Sylvia T. Wagner Professor of Public Affairs at the University of Wisconsin-Madison’s La Follette School of Public Affairs.

The average employer-sponsored family health plan now costs $28,303. Workers see about a quarter of this cost in their paycheck and assume that their employer pays the rest. The rude shock is that workers pay all of it.

When an employer thinks about hiring someone, they think in terms of total compensation, not the individual buckets such as cash wages, paid leave, retirement benefits, workers’ compensation premiums, and health insurance. When the cost of one of these items balloons, the others grow less. Economists have documented the trade-off between wages and fringe benefits for decades. Thus, inevitably, rising health insurance premiums crowd out cash wage growth.

Nowadays, the cost of an average family health plan is 44 percent of the typical full-time worker’s (pre-tax) cash wages. You would think somebody would push back on these costs on behalf of workers. Sadly, almost no one is. The real question is why, and what can be done about it.

It’s important to clarify that roughly 100 million people get their health benefits from large companies that self-insure their health plan. That is, the employer doesn’t buy health insurance; rather, it pays the health care bills for its workers and family members. So this is not a story about insurers gouging employers on premiums. Insurers are just hired administrators.

Instead, let’s start with the people large employers are paying to design their benefits. Most large self-insured companies use a handful of big benefits consultants to coordinate and manage health benefit design and contracting. There’s a very good chance these consultants look out for their own interests first and foremost, rather than the companies’, let alone the workers’ interests.

Begin with how “value” is measured. For hospitals, the standard approach is to examine the discounts hospitals provide off their billed charges. This almost makes sense, but hospital charges are widely known to be nonsense values set by the hospitals themselves and charged to virtually no one. Highmark, a Blue Cross plan, makes this exact point in its own employer materials: a facility that charges $100 and gives a 60% discount is paid $40, while one that charges $70 and gives a 50% discount is paid $35. The bigger discount costs more. Milliman, an actuarial firm, notes that charges are far less constrained than negotiated prices and thus rise faster, so discounts appear to grow larger at the same time prices rise.

The same pattern is evident throughout the health plan. Out-of-network claims are often repriced by vendors paid a percentage of the “savings” off billed charges, as a 2024 investigation of MultiPlan documented. The higher the bill, the bigger the fee. Drug benefits have long been judged by rebates off list prices set by manufacturers.

In every case, the rewards go to whoever sets the highest list price. The price that matters is the price actually paid for health care, net of any discounts. This is the equivalent of withholding more in taxes throughout the year only to be delighted with your large tax refund next year. Employers need to judge prices against a benchmark the provider doesn’t control, such as Medicare prices.

Additionally, large companies need to interrogate their benefits consultants on how exactly they are being paid. Federal law requires that brokers and consultants disclose their direct and indirect compensation, but not necessarily how the incentives are structured. If benefits consultant revenue rises with employer spending, or is higher for the vendors it recommends, employers have their answer.

What about the corporate benefits department? Isn’t it their job to directly interface with the consultants and monitor this? They need shaking up, because their incentives are all wrong. Corporate benefits staff are in a difficult position. If health plan changes go wrong, they get all the complaints, often with the CEO copied. If their decisions save the company (and its workers) millions of dollars, they get none of that. From their perspective, there is only downside risk. So they avoid any change that might generate complaints. Nobody gets fired for sticking with the status quo.

Meanwhile, workers are paying the bill. But their costs are diffuse and nearly invisible. Their share of the health plan cost is commonly spread across 26 paychecks. That’s a few hundred dollars per biweekly pay period. This is minimally salient to them. This is the classic case of concentrated blame and diffuse, hidden costs. Absent some outside pressure to change, the benefits office is doing exactly what its incentives reward.

None of this requires new legislation. It does require a sustained, CFO-level effort, because anyone else will bear the brunt of any pushback and get none of the reward. The following represents the minimum necessary steps to take charge of the situation:

Everyone in the employer health care supply chain does better when spending rises with minimal pushback. Hospitals, physicians and pharma all gain from higher prices. Insurers have little reason to push for lower net prices if payers focus on discounts from make-believe list prices. Benefits consultants paid a percentage of premiums or bonuses for steering clients to the same insurer earn more as costs climb. The only people who gain nothing are the ones paying the bill: workers.

Employers are not only stewards of their workers’ health care dollars, but they also have a fiduciary responsibility to run health plans in the best interests of their employees. It is time they took that role seriously.

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 18, 2026 at 12:47 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 11:47 am

— Weiwei Yang has left Microsoft after more than a decade to co-found a startup that is “building the power grid for the AI age,” according to her LinkedIn profile.

Yang was most recently a senior director with Microsoft Research, working on grid technology. Her team built a grid dataset and released small foundation models to help users operate and expand electrical infrastructure.

Yang thanked her community at the tech giant, adding, “I hope the relationships and collaborations we’ve built continue well beyond Microsoft, and that we find many new ways to work together.”

— Allie Mellen has joined Microsoft as principal director for security research and threat intelligence. Mellen was previously a principal analyst at Forrester. She also wrote “Code War,” a book that explores cyberattacks as a powerful geopolitical weapon.

In her new role, Mellen said she will lead strategy for protection and threat intelligence, “helping shape what intelligence we produce, how AI can improve its speed and quality, and how we turn that knowledge into better protection for customers.”

— Agility Robotics, the Salem, Ore., company that had its Nasdaq debut earlier this month, has announced three leadership changes:

— Former tech executive Drew Sheriff has been named CEO and president of the Space Needle and Chihuly Garden and Glass. Sheriff was previously a vice president at DoorDash and has held leadership roles at Amazon, Starbucks and Parachute Home. His roles focused on customer experience, product growth, strategy and marketing.

“His skill set is the ideal background for charting how we attract customers and how we delight customers in this new age,” Jeff Seely, board chair for the Space Needle and Chihuly Garden and Glass, told the Seattle Times.

— Microsoft has named Caroline King as director of its Washington state community and philanthropy team, with a focus on advocacy work across housing, affordability and other priority issues.

King is the founder and past CEO of Washington STEM, an organization that coordinates research, advocacy, policy, philanthropy and partnerships to support science, technology, engineering and math education in the state. She most recently served as a leader on the governing body of an international school in Luxembourg.

— Longtime Amazon and Microsoft tech exec Scott Wiltamuth has retired — mostly.

Wiltamuth joined Amazon in 2011 as an AWS vice president overseeing a large organization building developer and management tools. In 2018, he took a seven-month leave for colon cancer treatment. After returning, he sought a director-level position and thanked company leaders for helping him find a better fit. “Their flexibility and creativity enabled me to extend my AWS career,” he said.

Wiltamuth launched his tech career at Microsoft in 1993 and left nearly 19 years later as director of program management for Visual Studio Pro.

He now spends time with his wife and family, traveling, golfing, swimming and reading. “I don’t plan to pursue another full-time operational role,” Wiltamuth said, “but may do some part-time work.”

— Adam Nygate has exited Palo Alto Networks to co-found and lead a stealth startup based in Seattle. He was founder and CEO of Huntr, a platform launched in 2019 where security researchers could submit information on AI and machine learning vulnerabilities. Protect AI acquired Huntr, and Palo Alto Networks later acquired Protect AI.

“Huntr was a bet that open source gets safer when vulnerabilities are visible to the people who can fix them, even when that made life uncomfortable for vendors who’d rather keep things quiet,” Nygate said in a post announcing his career change and impending new baby.

— BluePill, a Seattle-based marketing startup that helps brands predict consumer behavior, has named Mike Weis as chief revenue officer and head of sales.

Weis has 40 years of experience in consumer packaged goods, retail and commerce, beginning his career as a Pacific Northwest leader at Unilever and holding executive positions at Catalina and Quotient Technologies. Recent roles include adviser at Contento2, eGateway Capital and And1 Advisors.

“Beyond the incredible résumé, Mike is one of the kindest, most genuine, and most passionate people I’ve met. Someone who has accomplished so much, yet brings so much humility, curiosity, and energy to every conversation,” said Ankit Dhawan, CEO and founder of BluePill.

— Glacis, a Seattle startup that builds tamper-proof records of AI behavior, has named Caer Mistral Sanders as a technical co-founder. Sanders has launched startups and joins Glacis from Thoughtworks. Before that, she held leadership roles at Wayfair and Onshape. As a teenager, she published a book on mixed-reality control systems and won a world robotics championship.

In a post announcing the new role, Sanders said she has designed medical record systems, researched robot communication, patented cryptographic technology and built widely used AI platforms. “This is the first time in my career I get to bring all of those skills to bear on one problem, and I couldn’t be more excited!” she added.

— The PNW Battery Collaborative has welcomed Jason Demeny as its director of communications. Demeny is a marketing leader whose past employers include Crusoe, Patch, Qualtrics and Apptio. Earlier in his career, he spent more than a decade at Microsoft over two stints, most recently leading teams that served the Azure Partner Experience group.

The nonprofit PNW Battery Collaborative brings together startups, innovators and researchers focused on energy storage.

— Tom Wheeler, former chairman of the Federal Communications Commission, has joined the advisory council for Known, a Bellevue, Wash.-based company building accountability infrastructure for autonomous AI. Wheeler led the FCC from 2013 to 2017.

Known, previously called Identity Digital Innovation Labs, spun out of Identity Digital in September.

— Versium has promoted Matthew Baumgartner to vice president of engineering. The Redmond, Wash.-based company provides data and software that help businesses identify potential customers, fill in missing contact information and target their marketing. Baumgartner has been with Versium since 2018.

— Charlie Trillingham has been named communications manager for the University of Washington AI and Machine Learning for Engineering programs and the UW NSF AI Institute for Dynamic Systems. He previously served as a marketing and communications lead for the Buerk Center for Entrepreneurship within the UW’s Foster School of Business.

#5447. ‘The bottleneck used to be dumpling-folding talent’: Din Tai Fung CEO on America’s top-grossing restaurant chain turning craft into corporate training

The restaurant chain with the highest per-store sales in America says the thing that used to limit its growth was a labor shortage of a very specific kind. Anyone who’s had the soup dumplings at the memorable chain can attest to seeing the lab-coated technicians behind the glass windows working their magic.

“The bottleneck used to be dumpling-folding talent,” Albert Yang, CEO of Din Tai Fung North America, told Fortune by email. “But through continuous improvements to our training programs, we’ve largely overcome that challenge.”

Dumpling-folding talent is a phrase with a lot of history behind it. For most of the time Chinese food has been sold in America, the people folding it were family: the owner, the spouse, the kids and, as Lucas Sin, chef at the New York chain Junzi Kitchen, put it in a 2020 Fortune roundtable, “a cousin of a cousin of a cousin from Fujian.”

At Din Tai Fung, folding is now a corporate job track: a 12-week training program, and a dumpling training manager in every U.S. restaurant, Yang told the Los Angeles Times in 2023.

That swap, from family labor to systems, is reshaping Chinese food in America. Din Tai Fung’s U.S. restaurants averaged $27.4 million in sales in 2024, nearly double the next-closest chain, according to Technomic data reported by Restaurant Business. Panda Express, co-run by an engineer who built her own point-of-sale system in the 1980s, now tops $6 billion a year.

The old Chinese-American restaurant, as the people who ran it describe it, depended on cheap labor at the start and a ready buyer at the end.

Foreign Policy reported in 2019 the waves of migrants from rural Fujian, who had staffed takeout kitchens in the 1980s and 1990s had died down as living conditions in China improved. Wages for takeout cooks had climbed from about $1,500 a month in the 1980s to close to $4,000. The family side ran out too. A 2019 New York Times analysis of Yelp data found Chinese restaurants fell from 7.3% to 6.5% of all restaurants across the 20 largest U.S. metro areas over five years, about 1,200 fewer places, as owners retired and their college-educated kids took other jobs.

“There was no succession plan, because success was seen as not having to do it anymore,” Jason Wang, cofounder of Xi’an Famous Foods, said in the Fortune roundtable.

The pressure hasn’t eased. In 2025, chain restaurant sales grew at their slowest pace outside the pandemic since the Great Recession, and Restaurant Business listed an immigration crackdown among the reasons, along with weak consumer confidence, weight-loss drugs and bad weather, in its Technomic Top 500 coverage.

Yang tells the demand side through his own childhood. Many Americans, he said, first met Chinese food at cheap fast-food and fast-casual spots opened by immigrants who couldn’t afford beautiful dining rooms.

“They were focused on surviving, supporting their families, and building a future for the next generation,” he said.

But now, the Chinese food offered by his family’s company is downright aspirational.

“I remember growing up, my mom would pack me Chinese food for lunch, and other kids would sometimes make fun of me for it,” he said. “Now, I hear from parents that their kids actually think it’s cool when someone brings leftover Din Tai Fung to school for lunch.”

Din Tai Fung was inducted into the Asian Hall of Fame this month as a “Global Family Legacy” honoree; Albert and Aaron Yang accepted on behalf of the family at the Nov. 5 ceremony in Los Angeles.

The Chinese food businesses that have scaled in America are the ones that replaced family labor with process early.

Panda Express is a top example. Andrew Cherng’s family opened Panda Inn in Pasadena in 1973, and business was so slow at first his mother would sprinkle salt on the threshold to chase off evil spirits, he said at Nation’s Restaurant News’ CREATE conference in July. His wife, Peggy Cherng, is an engineer by training. When point-of-sale systems barely existed in the mid-1980s, she built one.

“We had to develop it ourselves,” she said. Panda now has more than 2,600 U.S. locations, more than $6 billion in annual sales, and its own Panda University for employees—ranking it 11th among U.S. chains.

People in the business saw this coming years ago.

“Automation and central kitchens will take over,” Wong of the culinary federation told Foreign Policy in 2019. Zhao predicted takeouts would be consolidated under new brands that keep prices low through automation.

The newest arrivals come with systems already built. Chinese chains including HeyTea, Chagee, Luckin Coffee, Wallace, and Haidilao, some with thousands of stores at home, have pushed into U.S. cities to escape a price war in a saturated home market, the Times reported in December 2025.

“China’s food service industry is suffering from severe oversupply,” Bob Qing, founder of the restaurant investor Tomato Capital, told the paper. Limited-service Asian and noodle chains grew U.S. sales 7.8% in 2025, faster than any other segment, according to Technomic data reported by Restaurant Business.

Din Tai Fung is the cleanest example, because its whole product is the thing that’s hardest to systematize. Each Din Tai Fung restaurant turns out about 10,000 dumplings a day with roughly 30 chefs on rotation, each dumpling held to 18 folds and 21 grams, the LA Times reported in 2023. Kan Kuang-Ming, the chain’s head chef in Taiwan, told the paper: “You have to fail about 1,400 times before you can make one that is beautiful.”

In Taiwan, new chefs learn by shadowing a senior chef. In the U.S., they go through a training program instead.

“Our current training program is 12 weeks, though it still takes six months and up to a year to get up to speed,” Albert Yang told the Times then. Entry-level hourly jobs started at $20 an hour, he said, and managers at $100,000.

The family business started the old way. Founder Bing-Yi Yang opened a cooking oil shop in Taipei in 1958, according to Restaurant Business, and later hired a Shanghai-born chef to make soup dumplings, the LA Times reported. When his son Frank opened the first U.S. location in Arcadia, Calif., in 2000, the grandsons worked the register.

“We were running credit cards when we could barely even see over the counter,” Aaron Yang told the paper.

Albert Yang now says the system is far enough along to speed up. Din Tai Fung opened three U.S. restaurants this year, in Irvine and Brea, Calif., and Scottsdale, Ariz. Yang credited years of spending on the company’s people, leadership development, training programs, operational systems and production capabilities.

Asked about a ceiling, he told Fortune: “I don’t believe in setting an arbitrary limit.”

The constraint he names now is the company’s own standards.

“Today, our bottleneck isn’t necessarily a physical or operational constraint,” he said. “It’s a self-imposed one driven by the quality standards we’re unwilling to compromise.” The other is real estate: A Din Tai Fung typically needs 10,000 to 20,000 square feet, which he called “incredibly challenging” to find in a prime spot in Manhattan or Brooklyn.

But for New Yorkers who had to wait many years before the first location opened in the Broadway district, in the former Mars 2112 space, the wait is already ending for location number two: The next one is set for Downtown Brooklyn, where Din Tai Fung has signed for 20,000 square feet in The Brook, a 52-story tower at 567 Fulton St., scheduled to open in 2027, according to the Brooklyn Paper.

Nick Lichtenberg is business editor and was formerly Fortune's executive editor of global news.

#5446. ‘Sister isn’t free’: Melinda French Gates fact-checks viral ‘SNL’ sketch on eldercare

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 1:23 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 1:23 pm

A “Saturday Night Live” skit about caring for aging relatives touched a viral nerve after it aired over the weekend, including with Melinda French Gates, who offered her own “fact check” on the too-close-to-home comedy.

The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.

French Gates wrote on Instagram this week that the sketch “is funny because it’s a little too true.” Using research from Pivotal, her investment and philanthropic organization, she went through the ad’s claims one by one and found that most held up:

Sister will provide. True, French Gates said, citing AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Among adults ages 55 to 64, women are nearly 40% more likely than men to care for an older relative, and nearly 40% more likely to provide constant care.

She’ll quit her job. “Mostly true,” at least the job part. Catalyst found that 42% of women who voluntarily left jobs in 2025 cited caregiving as the main reason.

Paid help is pricey. “True, unfortunately.” New America puts the average home health aide at more than $6,600 a month, and 24-hour care can top $25,000.

Sister may break down. Also true. In the Caregiving in the U.S. 2025 report, nearly two-thirds of caregivers said they were under moderate or high emotional stress, and women felt the strain more than men did.

“Free” is misleading. French Gates said Sister isn’t free; she’s the one paying for the care, in lost wages, stalled careers, thinner retirement savings and less time for her own life.

French Gates has made women’s health and caregiving central to her work since she stepped down as co-chair of the Gates Foundation in 2024.

She left with $12.5 billion to put toward her work on behalf of women and families. Much of that work runs through Pivotal, the Seattle-area organization she founded to handle her philanthropy and investments. In June she pledged another $215 million for women’s health, which brought her giving in that area to more than $600 million over two years. The pledge included $10 million to the Menopause Society for better menopause care in the U.S.

The sketch has been shared widely across the country this week, in part because it lines up so closely with the research.

In its own analysis, The New York Times cited studies showing that daughters generally provide at least twice as much care to aging parents as sons do. The U.S., unlike many wealthy countries, offers no federal paid leave or long-term care insurance for family caregivers.

French Gates said she welcomed the conversation.

“I’m so glad we’re talking about this, and laughing about it,” she wrote on Instagram. “We need more honesty about what caring for loved ones really takes and why so much of that work falls to women. But I’d love for the day to come when these jokes don’t pack quite the same punch — because we’ve made it so much easier to care for the people we love.”
